./.title: PULSE Documentation
./.body:
PULSE Documentation
Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine is a marketing agency in an app: it checks how your business looks online, plans campaigns, writes and makes the posts, and publishes them only after you approve, on models that run on Runink's own platform.

Our own models · no third-party AI
Your marketing agency in an app
PULSE checks how your business looks online, plans campaigns, writes and makes the posts, and publishes them only once you approve.
Get started

Brand Analysis: One check-up of your site and your market: your score, the fixes to make, who could buy from you, who you compete with and what people search for.
Campaigns: Every campaign on one board of action cards, from planned to sent, with each post's steps traced on its campaign's page.
Studio: Posts, carousels, Instagram Reels and Stories, YouTube Shorts and documents in your brand colours, checked before you see them, ready to download or publish.
Leads and public tenders: People who could buy from you and public tenders that ask for websites, apps and content, on one board.
Measured, never made up: Every figure comes from a source PULSE read. What it could not read says “not measured”, never 0.
Connect your accounts: Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, Search Console, Google Analytics and Ads, and your website's repository, from Settings.
Run and configure: Setup for each connector, the publishing switches and their arming order, and the full API.

docs/.title: Overview
docs/.body:
Overview

Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine. Your marketing
agency in an app. A small business loses its week to working out what to post,
where and for whom, then writing it, posting it, answering comments, chasing
leads, and checking whether any of it worked. PULSE does that work, and you
approve what goes out.
You give it your website. A check-up reads your site and the web and shows,
on Brand Analysis, how your business looks online: your site score, whether
AI answers and Google name you, your competitors, partners and leads. From
that, PULSE makes a 90-day plan and campaigns, writes the posts for your
approval, finds leads and public tenders, runs outreach sequences from your own
mailbox, and shows what came of it.
PULSE shows only figures it actually measured. A number it could not obtain
reads Not measured, never 0 and never an estimate. Every AI step runs on
the platform's own models; PULSE calls no outside AI service.
Who uses it



Who
What they do
Guide




Owners and marketers
Run check-ups, approve posts and emails, work leads
User guide


Your PULSE administrator
Manages access and roles, connections and the switches that let PULSE publish, send or call

Developers
Call the API, connect a website form or chat, build on PULSE
Developer guide



Availability

Warning: What is built and what is not yet available.

PULSE is an Android app. An iOS app is planned and not yet built.
There is no web app.
PULSE is not yet available on Google Play, the App Store or any cloud
marketplace. Runink installs it for approved organisations.
Sign-in is Google only, for accounts Runink approved. There is no open
sign-up. Roles (viewer, editor, admin) come from your organisation's
subscription on Runink's TIDDE platform; admins are added by Runink.
Everything that goes outward (publishing, email, calls, messages, the
website chat) is off by default and stays off until an administrator
arms it and a person approves each action.
Google Business Profile and reviews are built but not yet available:
Google has not yet granted API access.

For prices and plans, see the PULSE product page.

PULSE's logo is its persona: the puppy running over a heartbeat line, shown in
the corner of these pages and on the app's sign-in screen. Runink is the
company that makes PULSE, so the app and these pages say PULSE by Runink.

Concepts: Measured and not measured, the plan gate, approval and publishing, personas.
Architecture: The parts of PULSE and how they fit.
User guide: Every feature, one page each, with its status.

Developer guide: The API, extension points, and building PULSE.

docs/concepts/.title: Concepts
docs/concepts/.body:
How PULSE works

Four ideas explain almost everything you see in Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine.

Measured and not measured: Why PULSE shows “Not measured” instead of a 0 or a guess.
The plan gate: The model proposes; a reviewer checks it against the evidence before it is kept.
Drafts, approval and publishing: How a post goes from an idea to sent, and every switch on the way.
Personas: Who you talk to, taken from your check-up and your leads, never invented.

In one paragraph. PULSE measures what it can (your site, the web, the
accounts you connect, its own records), says plainly what it could not
measure, and proposes work from that: a plan, campaigns, posts, replies,
leads. Every proposal is checked, by rules and by a reviewer, before you see
it. Nothing leaves PULSE until you approve it, and not even then unless your
administrator has switched publishing on.
For administrators and developers

Architecture: One process, one port, the call chain, and where data lives.
Sovereign inference: One shared model server, time budgets, and grounding.
Agent activity: The live feed of what every agent is doing.

docs/concepts/measured-and-not-measured/.title: Measured and not measured
docs/concepts/measured-and-not-measured/.body:
Measured and not measured

PULSE shows a figure only when something measured it. A figure nobody measured
is not drawn as 0 and is not estimated: it says Not measured, or shows —.
A 0 is a real answer ("we looked and there were none"); "not measured" means
nobody looked.
The answers you will see



What the app says
What it means




A figure
A source answered: your site, the web, a platform, a connected account, or PULSE's own records.


Counted
From PULSE's own records (posts sent, drafts approved, tasks done). A 0 here is a real 0.


Nothing found / None in the last 28 days
The source answered and had nothing.


Not measured / —
No source answered. No figure is shown.


Needs a connection / Connect …
Only an account you have not connected can answer it.


Could not be read
The source exists but did not answer right now, usually with the reason. Try again later.


Not recorded
It happened, but PULSE kept no record of it.


not yet
It has not happened.



Three of these are easy to confuse, and the app keeps them apart on purpose:
an empty answer, no answer, and an answer that could not be read. A page
that could not read something says so rather than showing an empty list.
Where the figures come from



Source
Examples




Your check-up
Site score, AI and search visibility, Google Discover readiness, leads, competitors, partners


PULSE's own records
What PULSE did: posts sent, drafts approved, outreach drafted, tasks done


The platforms
Each post's results as Instagram, LinkedIn or YouTube report them


Accounts you connect
Google Analytics, Google Ads, Google Search Console


You
Your weekly reviews on the 90-day plan, your own figures for its targets, deal values



A figure a platform does not report for a kind of post is "not measured" for
that post, never 0.
Lines over time
A line is drawn only through measured points, and starts once there are two.
A day or a check-up that measured nothing is a gap, not a 0.
When the model estimates
Some numbers are the model's judgement, not a measurement. The app labels them
as such, for example a trending topic's heat … (model estimate) or a
content gap's demand and opportunity scores. A lead's fit tier (high, medium,
low) is not a probability.
In a report, the figures come from your measured records. See
Reports.

docs/concepts/plan-gate/.title: The plan gate
docs/concepts/plan-gate/.body:
The plan gate

The plan gate reviews before anything is kept. Before PULSE keeps a
proposal, PULSE's reviewer checks it. The app calls it "PULSE's reviewer";
these docs call it the plan gate.
What the verdict does



Verdict
In the app
Effect




Agreed
"The reviewer agreed with it."
Kept.


Could not judge
"The reviewer could not check it, so it is not approved by the reviewer."
Kept, and marked. It is never shown as agreement.


Disagreed
Withheld / held back, with the reason
Not kept. It is listed as withheld, never shown as a proposal.


Switched off
"The reviewer is switched off on this server."
Kept without review, and marked.



"Could not judge" covers every case where no verdict was reached.
Where you meet it

Your check-up: the plan in the diagnosis, and the New groups of
customers to try (withheld ones are not shown).
Content ideas: ideas that do not pass are listed as held back, with the
reason.
Studio drafts written by a skill: the verdict is shown under What
PULSE checked.
Campaign plans: "PULSE's reviewer checked this plan against your audit",
or why it could not.
Site fixes: a pull request the reviewer does not agree with says
Withheld by the plan gate, and nothing is opened.
Autopilot replies: a reply goes out by itself only when PULSE's safety
rules and the reviewer both agree; otherwise it waits for you.
Automations the assistant proposes and AI calls.

The plan gate is one check among several. Skills also run their own checks (see The checks). One of them reads the draft against the facts you gave it, and never shows a draft that states figures, dates or names that are not in them. None of them publishes anything: that still needs your approval and the publishing switches.
For administrators
The gate is on by default. PULSE_JUDGEMENT=off turns it off: proposals then
pass unjudged and the app says the reviewer is switched off. In the API, judged messages carry a judgement
field and responses a judgements set listing every verdict, kept or withheld
(accepted=false). See Common types and
Configuration.

docs/concepts/drafts-approval-publishing.title: Drafts, approval and publishing
docs/concepts/drafts-approval-publishing.body:
Drafts, approval and publishing

Every post PULSE prepares goes the same way, and you can follow it on its
step trail:
Planned → Drafted → Approved → Scheduled → Sent, or
Withheld, Failed or Missed.
1. Planned
A campaign's plan, or your check-up, holds the idea of a post: its topic,
format, who it is for and when. It sits in the Planned column of
Campaigns. It is not written yet, so it cannot
be approved or scheduled.
2. Drafted
PULSE writes it, from the plan, from your check-up, from a campaign's daily
drafts, or because you asked in Studio. The draft is
checked (the skill's checks, PULSE's safety rules, the
plan gate) and lands in Drafts to approve.
Nothing is posted at this stage.
3. Approved
You approve it, on the Campaigns board, in Studio, or through the assistant
(which asks you to confirm). Only an editor or admin can approve. Approval is
the only way a post moves on: PULSE never publishes a piece nobody approved.
4. Scheduled
An approved post gets a time:

the time you pick when you move it to Scheduled;
its planned time, if it already had one still ahead;
with Autopilot on for that
account, the account's best time (never before the post's planned time);
with Autopilot off and no time, it goes out at once.

A post whose time passes while it still waits for approval is Missed. It is
never sent late; reschedule it.
5. Sent, or held back
When the time comes, PULSE checks, in that moment, everything that must agree:



Check
Who controls it




The channel is one PULSE can post to
PULSE: Instagram, LinkedIn, YouTube, your website's blog, the podcast and audiobook feed


The account is connected
You, in Settings → Integrations


The channel is Active
You, on its card


Publishing is switched on for the whole PULSE (the kill switch)
Your administrator


Publishing is switched on for that channel
Your administrator


For LinkedIn, the blog, the podcast and the audiobook: you are one of the named publishers
Your administrator



If all agree, the post goes out and moves to Sent, with its link where the
platform gives one. If one does not, the post is Withheld (held back) with
the reason, or Failed with the platform's reason. A withheld post is never
sent later on its own: fix the cause and schedule it again.
The Integrations card of each channel tells you in advance whether it can
publish (Ready to publish, or Can't publish: and why), so you do not
have to wait for a post to be held back to find out.
Posting it yourself
Any approved, scheduled or sent piece can be downloaded as files you post
yourself: the picture or video, and the caption. That is the way for Facebook,
X, email newsletters, or any channel you have not connected. See
Download.
Replies
Replies to comments, mentions and messages follow the same rule: drafted,
waiting for you under Replies waiting for you, sent only when you send them,
and only through a channel whose switches allow replies. The one exception you
can turn on is answering simple comments by itself,
limited to three kinds of reply, each checked first.
For administrators, every switch, its default and the safe order to turn them
on: Switches and arming order.

docs/concepts/personas/.title: Personas
docs/concepts/personas/.body:
Personas

A persona is a kind of customer you talk to, such as "wedding planners" or
"owners of small gyms". PULSE uses personas to decide who each post and each
content idea is for, and in what tone. PULSE never invents a persona: each
one comes from something you said or something PULSE found, and says where it
came from.
Where personas come from
In this order, with duplicates removed and at most five kept:

The campaign's audience, when the campaign names one.
Who buys from you, from your check-up: your answer to "Who usually buys
from you?", or what the check-up found.
The audience segments in your check-up's diagnosis.
Your leads' job titles: a title that at least two of your leads share
(the two most common).
The personas of your content ideas, which themselves come from what you
told PULSE, your leads, or the diagnosis's audience.

Where they are used

Campaign plans: each planned post is for one persona, written exactly as
above, and the plan gives each persona a tone (three adjectives and an
example line). The plan's checks flag any post written for someone who is
not on the list. You see the persona on each planned post as "For: …".
Content ideas: each idea is for one persona, with one problem and one
angle. See Ideas for what to post.

When there are none
With no check-up and no leads, PULSE does not know who you talk to, and it
says so instead of guessing. A campaign plan is then refused with: PULSE does
not know who you talk to yet: run a site audit (it asks who buys from you) or
add leads, then plan again.
To give PULSE better personas, answer Who usually buys from you? in your
check-up, set who you sell to under Fine-tune the content ideas, and
keep your leads' job titles filled in.

Note: The separate Persona Profile page left PULSE; its old addresses
(/persona-profile, /customer360, /intelligence-console) open Leads.

docs/concepts/sovereign-inference/.title: Sovereign inference
docs/concepts/sovereign-inference/.body:
Sovereign inference

Every AI feature in PULSE runs on the Runink platform's own inference server.
PULSE sends no prompt, no customer data, and no generated text to any
third-party model API.
One server for everything
All AI services share one inference server, so they share one set of agent
prompts and parameters. When INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL is set, PULSE uses the
shared inference plane at that address. Speech is provided by the platform's
own speech services, and PULSE embeds no speech engine.
If the inference server or its model is missing, PULSE still starts, and AI
features fail with inference server is not running instead of blocking the
whole app.
Which model
INFERENCE_MODEL names the model PULSE asks the server for. Set it to the general
model your inference server loads. Unset, PULSE requests the platform's default.
Every agent uses that one model. An agent's own configuration sets its
instructions, not its weights. See Model cards.
In a cluster the name is only a label: the model actually served is chosen by
the platform's inference deployment.

Note: Against a remote plane that takes the name at face value, INFERENCE_MODEL must match
what that server loaded. PULSE does not check.

Is the model ready

GET /health returns model_ready.
ModelService/GetModelStatus returns ready. The app polls it on startup.

A server that has started but is still loading counts as not ready.
Long generations
A long generation can take minutes, so PULSE allows a generous time for each.
If a generation cannot finish in the time allowed, PULSE says so instead of
returning a partial answer. When the server is busy, a request may be declined
with ResourceExhausted: the inference plane is at capacity and declined this
request; nothing was generated — retry in a few minutes.
Output screening
Everything PULSE can publish is screened before it reaches you, and nothing
is published without a person's approval. Operators can widen screening in
Configuration; a screened answer
arrives at once rather than token by token.

docs/concepts/agent-activity/.title: Agent activity
docs/concepts/agent-activity/.body:
Agent activity

A long generation can take minutes. The agent activity card shows it on every
screen, not only the one that started it. It is fed by
ActivityService.SubscribeAgentActivity.
What you see
Each run shows its agent (for example pulse:whitepaper), its status
(running, done, or failed), and its steps, in your language. A step you have
no line for in your language is not shown. An answer that was reused or that
was produced in a reduced mode is marked as such.
Whose runs you see
By default you see your own session's runs. The server uses the session
field of the request, or, when that is empty, the caller's x-agent-trace-id
header. Work that no request started (a schedule, an inbound message, a
background job) is not shown to a scoped subscriber.
Opening the page mid-run
A page opened halfway through a run still shows that run: when you subscribe,
the server first sends the runs in progress, then snapshot_complete, then
live events.
The featured strip
ActivityService.ListFeaturedMessages returns operator-written sponsor and
partner cards for the rotating strip. The server reads them from a file named by
FEATURED_MESSAGES_PATH. No file means an empty strip, not an error. You can
change the cards without rebuilding the app.

docs/architecture/.title: Architecture
docs/architecture/.body:
Architecture

For administrators and developers: the parts of PULSE and how they fit.
The parts



Part
What it does




The app
A Flutter app for Android (iOS is planned and not yet built). There is no web app. It talks to the backend over gRPC.


The backend
One Go server per deployment, on one port: gRPC for the app and API clients, plus a few plain HTTP routes (health, media, sign-in and OAuth callbacks, the website form and website chat, the podcast feed).


The store
Every table, account, session and media file, sealed under PULSE's own key on the platform's object store. There is no database. One writer, so one backend instance per deployment.


The models
The platform's own inference: open-weight models on Runink's own servers. PULSE calls no outside AI service. See Sovereign inference.


Speech and lip-sync
The platform's shared text-to-speech, speech-to-text and lip-sync services. PULSE embeds no speech engine.


The web reader
The platform's shared crawler reads public pages for check-ups, leads and market signals, with one identity and robots.txt obeyed. See Web reading.


Connections
The customer's own accounts (Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, Google, Microsoft 365, HubSpot, a website repository and others), each with the customer's own grant. Tokens are sealed.


TIDDE
Runink's platform runs the deployment: it installs PULSE, keeps the accounts and the subscription, and provides the shared services above.



Every call goes through the same chain
Every gRPC call is checked for authentication and authorization. Every method needs a valid session
except sign-in and the model status; the caller's role is checked against each
method on every call.
From proposal to action

An agent proposes work (a plan, a post, a reply, a lead) from measured
inputs.
The plan gate and the shared safety rules check
it before it is kept.
A person approves it (Drafts, approval and publishing).
It goes out only if the administrator armed that channel
(Switches).

Where data lives

All PULSE data is in its sealed store. Credential and personal fields are
sealed a second time, column by column, before they are written.
Deleting an account deletes its rows in every table that holds a person's
data. See Delete your account.

Configuration, switches and operations are in the
Admin guide; the API and extension points in the
Developer guide.

docs/user-guide/getting-started/.title: Getting started
docs/user-guide/getting-started/.body:
Sign in and first check-up

Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine does the weekly
marketing work of a small business: it works out what to post, where and for
whom, writes it, posts what you approve, answers simple comments if you let it,
finds leads, and tells you what came of it.
Your first ten minutes are one check-up: PULSE reads your website, asks you
a few plain questions, and fills the app with what it found. This page takes
you from the sign-in screen to that first check-up. It assumes your
organisation already has PULSE and that Runink approved your Google account.

Warning: Availability. PULSE is an Android app (an iOS app is planned and not yet
built). It is not yet available on Google Play or any marketplace; Runink
installs it for approved organisations. There is no open sign-up.


Sign in
Open PULSE. Until you sign in, every page sends you to the sign-in screen.
Choose Sign in with Google with the Google account your organisation
registered. Only approved addresses can sign in. See Signing in.
PULSE opens on Brand Analysis.

Start your first check-up
Before the first check-up, Brand Analysis says No check-up yet and what a
check-up shows: your site score, whether AI answers and Google searches name
you, and the leads and competitors PULSE finds.
Choose New site audit. The check-up asks one question per screen. Only the
first one is required; every other screen has Skip.

What's your website? PULSE opens that one page to read how the site
describes itself and which social pages it links to. If the page cannot be
opened, the next screen says so and the check-up carries on.
What do you sell? PULSE offers what it read on your site ("From your
website, we think you sell: …"). Choose Yes, that's right or change it.
Who usually buys from you? This is where your
personas start.
Where can people find you online? The pages found on your site are
offered; tap the ones that are yours, or type an Instagram name or a
LinkedIn page.
Who else sells something similar?
What do you want most right now? One of: Get more customers (the
default), Get found on Google, Bring back past customers, Reach
more people on social media, or Save time on posting.
Want to show us your shop? Photos, a short video, a price list or a
brochure, or a voice note. Each file says what PULSE could read from it.
See what you can attach.
Ready to check your business? Your answers as plain sentences; tap one
to change it. More details (optional) holds the type of business, what
you are best known for and anything else PULSE should know. Fine-tune the
content ideas (optional) sets who you sell to, where you post and how
deep the content research goes.

Choose Start my check-up. It takes a few minutes. You can close the screen
and carry on: the check-up keeps running, and the title line of every page
shows how far it got. See what we found opens the result.
You can also start a check-up by typing one line to the assistant:
Audit example.com. See Audit a domain.

Read what it found
When the check-up ends, Brand Analysis fills in. Start with the cards at the
top: each one is a page with a one-line answer and a dot that says whether
that answer was measured. Then read Needs you now: it lists the fixes
in your plan, the drafts waiting for your approval and the replies waiting for
you. See Brand Analysis.
The check-up also prepares work for you, and nothing of it goes out by itself:

Campaigns shows the campaign PULSE proposes, and the drafts it wrote,
waiting for your approval.
Leads shows the people the check-up found, in New, and your
follow-up tasks under To do today.


Connect your accounts (when you are ready)
A check-up needs no connected account. Connecting them is what turns "not
measured" into real figures and lets PULSE post what you approve. Open
Settings → Integrations. See
Connect your accounts.



Note: Nothing is posted until you approve it, and not even then while your
administrator has publishing switched off. PULSE's AI runs on your PULSE's own
model server, which serves everyone's requests in turn, so a generation can
take a few minutes, longer at busy times.

Next

Signing in
Brand Analysis
How PULSE works

docs/user-guide/sign-in/.title: Signing in
docs/user-guide/sign-in/.body:
Signing in

You sign in to PULSE with Sign in with Google. Only approved accounts get
in: your Google address must be on your organisation's list of allowed
addresses, which Runink keeps. There is no open sign-up and no self-invite.
Sign in with Google
PULSE never signs you in by itself when the app opens, so Sign out keeps
you out. The first time you sign in, PULSE makes you an account with the
viewer role, unless your role was set in advance (see below).
When Google sign-in does not let you in, the sign-in screen says why in your
language, for example:



What you see
What to do




Your address is not on this PULSE's list of people allowed to sign in
Ask your PULSE admin to have it added.


Nobody can sign in with Google on this PULSE yet
The allowed list is empty; ask your PULSE admin.


Your Google account's email address is not verified
Verify it with Google, then try again.


Google sign-in is not set up on this PULSE
Your administrator has not finished setting PULSE up; tell them.


This copy of the app is not registered with Google yet (Android)
Your administrator registers the app with Google; tell them.



Closing Google's sheet without choosing an account shows nothing.
What your role lets you do



Role
What it can do




Viewer
Read everything in your account. Cannot start a check-up, send, call or publish.


Editor
Everything a viewer can, plus run check-ups, make and approve content, send email and place AI calls (where your administrator allows them).


Admin
Everything, plus Admin (members and roles) and the messaging settings, reached from Settings → Account.



Roles come from your organisation's subscription, which Runink's TIDDE platform
keeps: it sets each listed account to editor or viewer, and a trial that has
ended or a cancelled subscription makes the account read-only. Administrators
are added by Runink, never by the subscription. The server checks your role on
every action, so a button you can see is not a promise that the action is
allowed. Administrators: see Users and access.
How long you stay signed in
The app renews your sign-in by itself for up to 30 days. It keeps it in the
device's secure store, never in a plain file.
Sign out is at the foot of the navigation rail. It ends that sign-in
everywhere it is used at once. To delete your account instead, see
Delete your account.
Where the session lives
For administrators and developers. The app holds an access token (24 hours)
and a single-use refresh token (7 days), sent as authorization: Bearer …, in
the platform keystore. There is no plaintext fallback: if the keystore refuses
the write, the session lasts only until the app closes. The session behind the
tokens lasts at most 30 days. See also
Users and access and the
HTTP endpoints.

docs/user-guide/ninety-day-plan/.title: 90-day plan
docs/user-guide/ninety-day-plan/.body:
The 90-day plan

The 90-day plan is first in the rail, under Plan. It is one thread
from your check-up to qualified leads: fix, then publish, then convert.
Every action comes from something your check-up found.
Status: built.
Make it
After your first check-up, choose Make my 90-day plan. The plan has three
30-day phases:



Phase
What it holds




Fix and foundations
Fixes from your site score, pages AI assistants cannot read, buyer questions the AI answers without naming you


Publish and attract
The pieces of your campaigns, Google Discover and retention items


Convert and scale
Follow-ups with the leads the check-up found and with inbound enquiries



Each action shows the finding it comes from, who owns it, the week it is due,
the automation that can help with it, and a link to where the work is done.
The plan creates nothing by itself: a post is still written and approved on
Campaigns, an email still waits for your send, a site fix still goes
through the site report.
Work the plan

Accept or Drop an action, Move to another week, or change its
owner. Your edits carry over to the plan of your next check-up.
This week on your plan (also on Brand Analysis) lists this week's
actions and how many wait for your yes.
The targets are set for your business. Each one shows where it comes
from (a public benchmark, with its source), or says it is assumed when no
benchmark was found. You can override a target.
KPIs come only from measured figures. One with no source reads Not
measured and says what would measure it.

Weekly review
Weekly review asks what went well, what did not, notes, and how satisfied
you are (out of 10). Earlier check-ins appear in the same list.
Inbound leads
Leads › Inbound lists the enquiries from your website form, your website
chat and HubSpot, scored for fit and intent with the reason for each point.
Move them from New to Qualified (marketing-qualified), Sales-accepted
(sales-qualified), then Won or Lost. Only your decisions are stored.

docs/user-guide/brand-analysis/.title: Brand Analysis
docs/user-guide/brand-analysis/.body:
Brand Analysis

Brand Analysis (/brand-analysis) is where PULSE opens: how your business
looks online, what PULSE did for you, and what to do next. It reads your latest
check-up and the accounts you connected. It shows only what was measured; a
figure nobody measured says Not measured, never 0.
A new session (after signing in, or opening or reloading the app) starts on
Let's run your first audit: the check-up's questions, one at a time (see
Sign in and first check-up). View History and
Open audit on that page show your earlier check-ups. Once you start or open
one, the page below is shown for the rest of the session.
Leads, Campaigns and Studio follow the same rule. Until you start or open a
check-up in the session, they show no check-up's leads, drafts, proposed
campaigns or pieces, and no page's title line shows an earlier check-up's
status. Once you do, they show what that check-up made. What earlier check-ups
made is never deleted: it is under From earlier audits on each page, one
click away. What you made, rewrote, approved or worked on yourself (a lead you
moved past New, a draft you edited) always stays in view.
At the top are New site audit (starts another check-up) and View History
(your check-ups). To type or speak a command, use the assistant; see
Assistant and voice.
The cards
Below the buttons, every part of Brand Analysis is a card, grouped in the
order you act on them. Each card gives its one-line answer from the check-up
and a dot:

Measured: PULSE has a real answer (it may be "nothing found").
Not measured: the check-up did not measure it, is still running, or that
part did not finish.
Needs a connection: only a connected account can answer it (for
Results, Google Analytics or Google Ads).




Group
Cards




Your plan
Your plan: fixes for your site and posts


Your leads
People who could buy from you · How likely your leads are to buy · Customers you might lose


Your market
Who you compete with · Where you win and where you lose · Partners to contact · New groups of customers to try


How people see you
Can people find you? · What people are talking about · How your business comes across · Ready for Google Discover


Ideas
Ideas for what to post


Results
Results · Your last check-up



Tap a card to open its page. Every page says which check-up it shows and when
it ran, and Brand Analysis takes you back. See
The Brand Analysis pages.
Your last check-up, and Needs you now
Side by side on a wide screen, one above the other on a phone:

Your last check-up: the site and when it was checked, then either
Everything was checked. or how many parts finished (the rest are tried
again on the next check-up). See how this was done opens every stage, where
each answer came from and the full text of anything that failed. Check
again starts a new check-up. Before the first one, this is where it says
No check-up yet.
Needs you now: one line and one button per thing waiting for you:

Your plan: N things to do, with See all;
N drafts wait for your review, with Review (opens the drafts on
Campaigns);
N replies wait for you, with Review (the replies Autopilot drafted).

When all three were read and none waits, it says Nothing waits for you
right now. If one could not be read, it says so rather than claiming
there is nothing.


When you look at an earlier check-up, a line above says Showing the
check-up of its date, with Show the latest.
The key numbers
One period selector, 7 / 30 / 90 days, sets the numbers below it. Each
number shows its change when the earlier period was measured too.



Number
Where it comes from




Site score
The check-up's score of your site, out of 100


New leads found
Leads PULSE found in the period, counted from its own records; tap it to open Leads


Named in AI answers
Of the AI answers the check-up read, how many cited your site ("N of M")


Times people saw you
Impressions your connected accounts reported in the period



Site score and Named in AI answers appear only once there is a
check-up; Times people saw you needs a connected source.
What PULSE did
What PULSE did is counted from what PULSE itself saved, so a 0 here is a
real 0, marked Counted. Nothing in it is estimated.

Posts published, per channel, drafts approved, outreach messages drafted,
follow-up tasks done, and leads contacted or moved on.
This week: replies sent (and how many PULSE sent on its own), the results
of your posts that the platforms reported, and what goes out next. A result
no platform reported says Results of your posts: not measured yet.
Email me this sends the week to you from your own connected mailbox.
Results measured: impressions, clicks, conversions, engagement and ad
spend for the period, with engagement by channel, from what your connected
accounts reported, and on how many days of the period they were measured. Without them it says Not measured and offers
Open Integrations.

Something PULSE keeps no record of says not recorded. For example, a post
sent at the moment you approve it is not yet counted here, and the card says
so.
How you are doing over time
How you are doing over time draws a line only for what has measured points
in the chosen days, and a line starts once there are two.



Line
Source




Site score over time · Named in AI answers over time · Searches where you appear · Google Discover ready
Your check-ups, one point each


Engaged visits · Page views
Google Analytics


Ad views · Ad clicks
Google Ads


Search clicks · Search impressions
Google Search Console


People who saw your posts
What LinkedIn and Instagram reported for your posts



What was never measured is listed on one line (Not measured yet: …), what
is connected but has no measured day yet on another, and each source you have
not connected gets one Connect button.
The forecast range under a Google Analytics line is marked Approximate range when fewer than 60 days of history were behind it: the range is still shown, and the real value may fall outside it more often than 1 in 20.
What this check-up measured, and your check-ups

What this check-up measured draws your site score as a gauge and every
dimension the check-up scored, each out of 100. Grey means not measured, not
zero.
Your check-ups appears once you have more than one. Tap a check-up to
see the whole page as it was then. You can delete one, or Clear all
previous check-ups (type your domain to confirm; the latest stays unless
you tick it). Deleting removes the check-up's steps, what it found and its AI
visibility results; your leads, campaigns, drafts and site-score history
stay. Start over removes every check-up and what it made; see
Start over.
Your material lists each file you gave the check-up as A1, A2 …, with
every finding that cites it.

Further down the page
Below the overview are Content ideas for your customers (see
Ideas for what to post),
short previews of what the check-up found about leads, competitors, partners
and new groups of customers, and one collapsed card per research area that
has something to show.

docs/user-guide/brand-analysis-pages/.title: Brand Analysis pages
docs/user-guide/brand-analysis-pages/.body:
The Brand Analysis pages

Each card on Brand Analysis opens its own
page (/brand-analysis?section=…). Every page names the check-up it reads and
its date, with a way to pick another check-up, and lists everything that
check-up kept, not just the preview on the card. Before your first check-up, a
page says so and offers to start one.
A page never fills a gap with a guess. It tells apart four cases: found,
nothing found (the source answered and had nothing), Not measured in
this check-up, and could not be read right now.
Your plan
Your plan: fixes for your site and posts (?section=plan).

Fixes for your site: what the site score found, highest impact first.
Your 30-day plan: the follow-up cycle the check-up made from its plan:
the week you are in, Tasks, week by week, a Calendar by channel, and
Where you started and where you are, which is measured only from your
weekly check-ins (you add them on Leads).

The open tasks are what Needs you now counts as "things to do".
The full list of checks and fixes is the site-score report. To have PULSE propose a site fix as a pull request on your own website
repository, see Website repository.
Your leads

People who could buy from you (?section=leads): every lead the
check-up found, with the contact its page publishes and where it was found.
Each has a fit tier (high, medium, low); it
is not a probability. The leads are on Leads in
New.
How likely your leads are to buy (?section=conversion) and
Customers you might lose (?section=churn): what that research area of
the check-up read, its status and a note, and where to act on it. Customers
you might lose is read from what your site offers existing customers
(sign-in, docs, support, newsletter …); churn itself needs customer data.

Your market

Who you compete with (?section=competitors): the competitors the
check-up named, with their channels.
Where you win and where you lose (?section=edge): how you compare
with each competitor. A site that could not be read is
not measured, never a loss.
Partners to contact (?section=partners): businesses, associations,
newsletters and shows the check-up found, with the email, phone or LinkedIn
their own page publishes, and the shows and channels you could appear on.
The same partners are on Leads → Partners.
New groups of customers to try (?section=niches): a few niches
next to yours, each citing its source. The plan gate withholds
the ones it disagrees with.

How people see you

Can people find you? (?section=searchAi): Your site score and its
parts; Can AI tools read your site; What AI answers
say when buyers ask (whether an AI answer cites you and which competitors it cites); Where
you show up in search results; and, once you connect Google Search
Console, Google searches (Search Console): clicks and appearances in the
last 28 days against the 28 before, your Top searches, searches Close
to the first page and Pages losing clicks.
Without Search Console it says Not measured and links to Integrations.
What people are talking about (?section=market): what the market
research measured and every trending post it saved, with its picture only
when one loads. A heat score is labelled as the model's estimate.
How your business comes across (?section=brand): Who buys from you
and What you sell, each marked with where it came from: your own
answers, your site, your leads, or the analysis.
Ready for Google Discover (?section=discover): which of Google's
Discover requirements your live page meets (HTTPS, mobile layout, large
image previews, a share image of at least 1200 px, article markup, a
publication date). Discover traffic itself is only in Search Console.

Ideas for what to post
Ideas for what to post (?section=ideas): first the topics your customers
look for that your site does not cover (content gaps), then the content
ideas: for one kind of customer, one problem and one angle, post ideas and the findings behind them. Ideas that did not pass PULSE's
checks are listed as held back, with the reason. How they are made:
Content ideas.
From the content gaps, PULSE may propose a campaign; it waits on
Campaigns.
Results

Results (?section=results): your measured figures for the period and
their impact. See Results and reports.
Your last check-up (?section=checkup): when it ran, how it went, and
every stage with what it did or why it did not, plus your other check-ups.
See how this was done (/site-audit/log) has the full log.

Old addresses
Addresses of pages that were merged into Brand Analysis still open here or on
Leads; they are listed on Old names and addresses.

docs/user-guide/site-score-report/.title: Site-score report
docs/user-guide/site-score-report/.body:
The site-score report

The site score on Brand Analysis comes from fixed, rule-based checks on
your live site, not from the model. Its full report, Site Relevance Audit,
is at /site-audit/report: every area, every check, and the fixes that would
raise the score. The app has no menu entry for it; open it at that address.
The score
Your site is scored in areas such as AI visibility, search visibility,
technical foundation, authority and trust, acquisition, engagement and
retention, which roll up into one overall score out of 100.
Each area also reports how much of it could actually be scored. Checks that
need a data source you have not connected are left out and listed under
Unconfigured data sources (excluded, not zeroed), never counted as zero.
The report shows the Category breakdown, the Biggest wins, and the
concrete fix-artifacts: a robots.txt, a canonical tag, a JSON-LD block, a
rewritten title. Green ones are safe to apply automatically; the others need a
person to review the copy or configuration.
Propose a fix as a pull request
With your website repository
connected, each fix has Propose as pull request. PULSE writes that one fix
on a new branch of your repository and opens a pull request for you to review
and merge. PULSE never merges and never changes your base branch. The
plan gate reviews the change first; if it does not
agree, the fix says Withheld by the plan gate and nothing is opened. One
fix gets one pull request, and the report shows its state as last read from
GitHub: Pull request open, Merged, Closed without merging, or No
pull request needed.
Apply the fixes to a server checkout
Apply to a repo is for administrators whose site checkout lives on the
PULSE server itself. Enter the repository's path on the server, then:



Button
Effect




Plan
Dry run: lists the file changes. Nothing is written.


Apply
Writes the files into that checkout.


Commit
Writes the changes and commits them on a branch.



Copy and infrastructure changes are never applied; they come back for a person
to review.

Warning: Proposing a pull request, and every button except Plan, works only for an
administrator, and only when your administrator has switched on both
publishing and site fixes for this PULSE. The path must be inside the
directory the administrator allowed. See
Switches and arming order and
Site pipeline.

docs/user-guide/audit-a-domain/.title: Audit a domain
docs/user-guide/audit-a-domain/.body:
Audit a domain

Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine can fill most of
its pages from one sentence. Type Audit and a web address into the
assistant, and PULSE reads the site, scores it, writes the diagnosis, and
copies the result into the pages that act on it. You do not have to know what
else to ask for.
Each stage on the way is tracked. A stage that wrote something says where its
result came from. A stage that could not finish says why, and the pages it would
have filled stay empty rather than showing something made up.
What you type
Open the assistant and send one line with a verb and a domain:
Audit example.com

The verbs PULSE recognizes are audit, analyse (or analyze),
scan, review, inspect, and score. A full address such as
https://example.com/pricing works too; PULSE keeps only the host name,
lower-cased.

A line that contains a question mark is treated as a question and goes to
the model as an ordinary chat turn. To run the audit, leave the question
mark out.
An IP address or localhost is refused with "…" is not a domain (expected
something like example.com).
Running an audit needs the editor or admin role. A viewer can read the
result but not start one. See
What each role may call.

The reply is a card titled Audit of example.com, with one row per stage.
Attach your own material
The new-audit form also takes photos or a short video of your store or
product, product documents and voice notes, so the audit compares your site
against them: what the material shows that the site does not say, where the two
disagree, and which benefits the site never communicates.



Kind
Accepted
Limits
What PULSE reads




Photo
JPEG, PNG, WebP (not HEIC: share it as JPEG)
15 MB
A description and the visible text


Video
MP4, MOV, WebM
60 MB, 60 seconds
Frames from the video, described like photos


Document
PDF, DOCX (50 pages, 20 MB); TXT, MD (2 MB)

The text. A scanned PDF has none; text recognition is not run


Voice note
WAV, WebM, OGG, M4A, MP3
20 MB, 5 minutes
A transcript



Each file is sealed in PULSE's encrypted store as it arrives; it is never kept
as a plain file. Only you can see your attachments. One that no audit used is
removed after 24 hours; one an audit used is removed 30 days after that audit
started. You can delete one at any time.
When something cannot be read, the attachment says so, and the audit does not
use it: image understanding unavailable (this deployment cannot read images), frames not analysed, transcription unavailable, or no text
found. PULSE never describes a photo it could not look at.
The Your attached material stage on the card lists what the diagnosis was
given. Findings that come from the material name the attachment they come from,
and are reviewed like every other part of the plan.
If an audit of the same domain is already running, a new audit with
attachments the running one was not started with is refused with an audit
of example.com is already running, rather than joining it without them. Your
attachments are kept: run the audit again when the current one finishes.
How long it takes
Minutes. When another audit is running on the same deployment, your
stages wait their turn, and the card shows Waiting for the model (position N
in the queue).
You can leave the page. The audit keeps running on the server, and each page
fills in as its stage finishes. When you come back to the assistant, the card
reconnects to the run.
While it runs, the title line of every page follows it: the domain, whether it
is still running and how it ended, and the reason the run gives. Tapping it
opens the check-up on Brand Analysis.
The stages
The card lists every stage of the audit as it runs, under the heading Running
— each page fills in as its stage finishes.



Step on the card
What it does
Where the result goes




Domain
Normalizes what you typed into the domain and the address to read.
—


Read the site, Site score, Search trends
Reads your live site, scores it, and looks up search interest in your business.
Brand Analysis › Can people find you?, and the site fixes in Your plan


Google Discover readiness
Checks Google's Discover requirements on your live page: HTTPS, mobile viewport, large image previews, a share image of at least 1200 px, article schema and a publication date. Discover traffic itself is only in Search Console.
Brand Analysis › Ready for Google Discover


Retention signals
Looks for what your site offers existing customers: sign-in, docs, support, changelog, community, newsletter, blog. Churn itself needs customer data.
Brand Analysis › Customers you might lose


Your attached material
Gives the diagnosis what your attachments contain, labelled as material you provided. Skipped when nothing was attached.
Your material on Brand Analysis, with the findings drawn from each file


Diagnosis
Writes the diagnosis of your market position and a plan. The plan is reviewed before anything is saved.
Brand Analysis


Drafts for approval
One draft per suggestion in the channel plan.
Campaigns, column Drafts to approve


Campaign
One campaign for this domain, linked to the diagnosis.
Campaigns


Publishing schedule
Puts the plan's dates on its drafts. Nothing is queued until you approve a draft; approving it while its date is still ahead schedules it then.
Campaigns (the date shows on each draft)


Creatives
One creative brief per suggested piece. Briefs, not finished media.
Studio › My Library


Course
One draft course built from the plan.
Studio › My Library (Learning)


Market summary
The diagnosis's positioning and competitive sections.
Brand Analysis › What people are talking about


Niche
The niche the rest of the research is about. When the diagnosis did not finish, it is read from your site's own text instead, and the stage says so.
—


Trending posts, Competitor channels, Guest opportunities, Leads
Research on the web for your niche. Each lead found gets a fit tier (high, medium, low); it is not a probability. Every lead lands in New with the contact its page publishes and where it was found, and is listed under Brand Analysis › People who could buy from you.
Brand Analysis (What people are talking about, Who you compete with, Partners to contact, People who could buy from you) and Leads


What you sell, Content ideas
What your site says you sell, quoted word for word, then the content ideas built on it. See below.
Brand Analysis › How your business comes across and Ideas for what to post


Visibility in GenAI answers
Measured by search only; no AI assistant is queried. Shows whether AI assistants can read your site and whether your business appears in the AI answers shown for buyer questions in your niche, with the sources cited and how you compare with competitors. A page that did not load is not measured, never not cited. Fixes are in the site score's actions.
Brand Analysis › Can people find you?


Content gaps
Where your content under-serves demand, by topic and format. Each gap cites the audit findings it is drawn from; its demand and opportunity scores are the model's estimates. PULSE proposes a campaign from them, for you to accept or dismiss.
Brand Analysis › Ideas for what to post, and the proposal on Campaigns


Competitors and where you win
Possible competitors, and where you win and where you lose against them. A site that cannot be read is not measured, never a loss.
Brand Analysis › Who you compete with, Where you win and where you lose


Partner contacts
Each partner found, with the email, phone and LinkedIn its own page publishes.
Brand Analysis › Partners to contact


New customer groups to try
A few niches next to yours. Each cites its source, and the plan gate judges them (withheld ones are not shown).
Brand Analysis › New groups of customers to try



Every figure in the stages from Drafts for approval to Market summary comes
from the diagnosis; none is invented along the way.
Guest opportunities whose address the search actually returned are kept with
their source and a Relevance (search fit) score, never a follower figure.
They show under Brand Analysis › Partners to contact. See
The Brand Analysis pages.
Content ideas for your customers (deep research)
At the end of a check-up PULSE turns what it measured into content ideas, shown on
Brand Analysis. Each idea is a scenario: one kind of customer, one problem they have,
one angle (teach, show proof, behind the scenes, offer, event), and the Instagram or YouTube
formats it suits, with post ideas and the findings that back it.

What it sells first. The offerings stage lists what your site says you sell, each
with the site's own words. The plan gate reviews them, and the check-up line says how many were kept and dropped. Ideas and
content-gap cards are tied to one of these.
What people search for. With Google Search Console connected, the searches
people type before they find your site, and where your site ranks for them, are
the first measured demand an idea can cite.
Who it is for comes from what you told PULSE, the leads the audit found, or the
diagnosis's audience. PULSE never invents a customer. See
Personas.
Each scenario is checked by the guardrails and the plan gate. Ideas that do not pass are listed as held back, with the reason.
Your Instagram week: a 7-day plan across several scenarios.

Tune (on the card, or Fine-tune the content ideas before a check-up) sets who you
sell to, what you sell, where you post, how often, topics to focus on or avoid, language,
region and depth. Quick is the default; Deep asks PULSE's model to think each idea
through first and takes longer. Saving on an existing check-up makes new ideas from the
same findings.
Start over
Settings › Account and the check-up history on Brand Analysis have Start over: type
your domain to delete every check-up of this account (or agency client) and what it
made: findings, content ideas, campaign suggestions you did not accept, drafts you did
not approve. You can also tick accepted campaigns, the leads check-ups found, and
approved or scheduled posts not sent yet. Anything published, its measured results and
your connected accounts are never deleted. It is refused while a check-up is running.
What each status means



Status
Meaning




done
The stage wrote at least one row, or a source that really answered found nothing. The row shows where the result came from: sourced from the web, inferred by the model, or sourced and inferred, plus the first source address.


failed
The stage ran and could not write anything, or had nothing to work from. The row gives the reason, for example had 4 to write, wrote 0 or no trend search answered (0 of 3 queries). The page it feeds stays empty.


skipped
The stage did not run. Either it was blocked because a stage it depends on did not finish (the reason starts with blocked:), or it is the publishing schedule and every channel it would queue on is switched off.


waiting
The stage is in the queue for the model, at the position shown.



A finding of "0" counts as done only when the source answered. When no
search answered at all, the stage is failed: silence is not reported as an
empty result.
Why "Publishing schedule" says skipped
The schedule stage puts each planned date on a draft of the same channel. It
queues nothing: a post waits for your approval, and approving a draft while
its date is still ahead schedules it for that date (on a channel that is
switched on). When the plan has no draft to put a date on, the stage ends
skipped with no draft to put the plan's times on (the tasks are on
the 90-day plan). That is not a fault
and does not make the audit partial.
A post whose date passes while it is still waiting for approval is marked
missed with the reason, and is never sent late: reschedule it from the
Scheduled column on Campaigns.
How the audit ends



Card heading
Meaning




Done — every page was populated
Every stage is done. The publishing schedule may be skipped.


Partly done — some pages are still empty (see the failed stages)
Some stages finished and some did not. The failed and blocked stages are listed with their reasons.


The audit failed
No stage that fills a page finished.



Resume, run again, or reuse

Resume the audit runs it again from the first stage that is not done.
Stages already done on the same input are not repeated, and nothing they
wrote is written twice.
Run it again starts a fresh audit even if one finished recently.
Asking again within 24 hours of a finished audit returns that audit as it
is, with a note saying when it ran. Use Run it again to force a new one.
Asking while an audit of the same domain is already running joins it. The
card says Joined the audit already running for this domain and replays
every stage from the start.

A fresh run never switches the campaign to active: it updates the one
campaign it keeps for this domain and leaves its status alone. It never
deletes or changes drafts that earlier runs left in Drafts to approve.
What is never inferred
The audit writes no performance numbers.

Results are not filled by an audit. Impressions, clicks,
conversions, and return come only from the accounts you connect.
Partners and shows found by an audit carry no follower, audience, or
engagement figure. Their score measures how well the show fits your niche,
and the label says so.
Audience sizes on the market pages are shown only when the search results
stated them. An unknown size stays unknown; it is never estimated.
The site score comes from deterministic checks on the live site. Checks
that need a data source you have not connected are left out and listed, not
counted as zero.

Where to see past audits
Every audit, with its stages and their reasons, is kept per user.
AuditPipelineService/ListAuditRuns lists yours, newest first, and
GetAuditRun returns one. See the
API reference.
On Brand Analysis, Your check-ups lists them with their date, how many
parts finished and their status. Tap one and the whole page shows it; the
latest is shown by default. Delete one, or Clear all previous check-ups
(type the domain to confirm; the latest stays unless you tick it). Deleting
removes the check-up's steps, what it found and its AI-visibility results;
your leads, campaigns, drafts and site-score history stay.

docs/user-guide/leads/.title: Leads
docs/user-guide/leads/.body:
Leads

Leads (/leads) is everyone outside your business in one page: everyone
who could buy from you (the people PULSE found and the
public tenders that need what you sell) on one board, and,
on the Partners canvas beside them, the partners, creators and shows you
work with. A switch at the top moves between the two.
From top to bottom, the Leads canvas has: the HubSpot import (when HubSpot is
connected), Who you're looking for, To do today, the counts, the
replies to your emails, the filter row, and the board.
The board
One board, five lanes: New, Talking, Proposal, Won, Lost.
People and public tenders share them:



Lane
A person
A public tender




New
found, not contacted yet
found by PULSE


Talking
contacted
interested, or preparing a response


Proposal
qualified: the offer is being made
response submitted


Won / Lost
the deal's outcome
the buyer's answer



Move on a card sets its lane. A move that means nothing for that kind of
card is refused, with the reason, and nothing changes: a tender is won or lost
only after you submitted a response (move it to Proposal first); a tender
you are not answering goes away with Not for us.
Each person is a card; tap it to open it. An open card shows the lead's
details, its next step, its History (the emails and AI calls to it) and its
action row:

Draft writes a message for this lead: a Cold email, a Cold-call
script or a LinkedIn DM. PULSE never sends a draft by itself.
Send (on an email draft) sends it from your own mailbox. See
Email.
Call places an AI call, where your
administrator has allowed them.
Move changes the lane.
Add deal value / Edit deal value records what the deal is worth.
Automate opens the lead's own automation; see
Automations.

A tender's card is described under Public tenders.
Filters
The filter row shows All, People or Public tenders. While tenders
are shown, it also narrows them by country and by type of work (what you sell
that the tender matched), and opens Tender settings.
Where leads come from



Source
How




Your check-ups
A check-up finds leads for your niche and puts them in New, with the contact their page publishes and where they were found.


Find → People who could buy from you
Finds businesses that publish a way to reach them and writes a first email, a call script and a LinkedIn message for each. It asks for a niche, a region, who buys from you, and competitors to leave out, filled in from your last check-up. 10 leads a run by default, at most 25.


Find → Public tenders: look now
Reads every tender source now. See Public tenders.


Add lead
By hand. A lead needs at least a name, an email or a company. On a phone with no signal, it is saved and marked Queued until you are back online.


Your website's contact form
Each enquiry becomes a lead in New. See Website form.


HubSpot
Sync from HubSpot imports your contacts. The bar says when it last synced and how many it read, or why it failed.



PULSE shows HubSpot's own lifecycle stage on a lead as it is, and does not
score HubSpot leads itself. The board lane is PULSE's own.
To do today
To do today lists, for each lead that is due, one next step in plain
words, such as "send a follow-up email" or "place an AI call to book a
meeting", with Do it and Skip (moves it to tomorrow). A lead with no
email or phone says so. It also lists:

the public tenders you are working on (not yet submitted) that close within
14 days, soonest first;
leads who replied to an email you sent, with the first words of the reply
and Answer;
leads PULSE's daily check says may go quiet, with its reason;
your Weekly check-in: new followers, posts, engagement, leads and how
satisfied you are this week, plus what worked and what didn't. Your
check-ins are what Your plan
measures progress with, and Recalculate my plan from these check-ins
re-plans the rest of the cycle;
what Autopilot needs from you, for example an account it stopped posting to
and why.

Deal value and won revenue
Moving a lead to Won asks what the deal was worth: an amount and a
three-letter currency code (such as EUR). A lead cannot be marked won
without a value. You can also give any open lead a value.
The counts above the board show Won this month (per currency, never added
across currencies), then, for New, Talking and Proposal, the open
value of the people in that lane and how many tenders are in it, and Tenders
closing within 14 days. Leads with no value are counted as "not valued",
never as 0; before PULSE first looked for tenders their counts say tenders
not counted yet, never 0. Deal values stay in PULSE; HubSpot receives
contacts only.
Email from your own mailbox
Connect your mailbox under Settings → Integrations → Email (Gmail,
Microsoft 365 or SMTP). Then Send on an email draft sends the newest draft
to the lead from your address, records it in the lead's history, and moves a
lead in New to Talking. Send asks you to confirm first. It is not
offered, and the sheet says why, when:

you are a viewer (sending needs an editor or admin);
your administrator switched email sending off;
no mailbox is connected, or it needs attention;
you reached the daily limit.

With Gmail or Microsoft 365, PULSE notices who replied and lists them under
To do today. With SMTP it cannot read replies, and the page says so.
Public tenders
Public tenders and requests for proposals that need what you sell (a council
website, an app, videos for a campaign) are cards on the Leads board. PULSE
reads official open tender data every day and matches it on what your
check-up found you sell. You decide, and you submit: PULSE reads and
drafts, and never submits anything.
Where PULSE looks



Source
Needs




EU tenders (TED)
Nothing


UK Find a Tender · UK Contracts Finder
Nothing


Brazil public purchases (PNCP)
Nothing


CanadaBuys
Nothing


Requests for proposals on the web
Nothing


US federal (SAM.gov)
Your own SAM.gov public API key, pasted on the SAM.gov card in Settings → Integrations



With Public tenders shown, the filter row says when PULSE last looked, and
Where PULSE looked says, for each source, what the last look got: notices
read, nothing new, could not be read (with the reason), or not
connected (with what to do). These are four different answers, never an
empty list.
PULSE looks once a day. Find → Public tenders: look now looks straight
away. If your administrator switched the daily look off, the page says so and
looking now still works.
A tender's card
Each tender's card shows a Public tender chip (Request for proposals
for a private buyer), the title, the buyer and country, the closing date with
how many days are left (No deadline stated when the notice gives none),
the source, and what it matched. While you work on it, it also says
Interested or Preparing. Open, it shows the value (Value not
stated when the notice gives none), the words and codes it matched on,
Open the notice, and its actions:

Prepare response writes a response draft (Draft again to redo it).
Move moves the card between lanes; in Talking it also marks it as
interested or as preparing a response.
Not for us sets it aside, with your reason.
Automate opens its own automation.

The response draft
Draft response (not sent) lays out: Why you, What the notice asks,
what is Answered, what is Not covered: add it yourself, Documents to
prepare, Before you send, the deadline and how to submit. Copy draft
copies it as plain text. Check it, complete it, send it yourself, then move the
card to Proposal. A draft PULSE's checks or reviewer refused says Not
drafted and why.
Tender settings
Tender settings sets the countries PULSE looks in (two-letter codes; empty
means all), notices too close to their deadline to bother with, reminders
before a deadline, the value range and its currency, public and private
buyers, whether new matches show in the bell, and whether PULSE drafts a
response for the best new matches by itself (this uses model time).
Partners
The Partners canvas lists the partners your latest check-up found, with how
to reach them and where they were found, then the partners, creators and shows
you follow. Add a partner adds one by hand. Each partner has Partnership
message, which drafts messages for you to copy and send yourself (PULSE does
not send these), and its own automation. Stop following removes a partner;
a later check-up that finds them again does not add them back.
Freelance & contracts
Freelance & contracts is a category of the Leads board, beside People
and Public tenders: everything that can bring money is in one place. Under
All its items sit in New with the rest, each card badged with its
category; in each lane the cards that state money come first. Save as
lead on an item makes it your own lead in New, valued from its published
total (a tender's estimated value) when it states one, else "not valued"; it
then moves New → Talking (Contacted) → Proposal (Qualified) → Won or Lost
like any lead and counts in the pipeline strip. An item you have not saved is
read when you open Leads and never stored.
The category lists contracts that match your expertise: the
skills buyers post contracts for, such as "data engineering", "AI
governance" or "Kubernetes". PULSE takes them from the check-up you opened in
this session:

what your site says you sell, and the skills its own words name;
what you named in Tune;
when those give little or the check-up could not read what you sell, the
skills your site's own product, service and pricing pages name.

The check-up's niche is never a term on its own; it only adds weight to a
term that shares a word with it. Each term shows where it came from and its
weight. Edit in Tune opens Tune, where Your expertise replaces the
inferred terms with yours (leave it empty to let PULSE infer them).
Under the category, a header shows those terms (Edit in Tune) and a
filter chooses the segment:

Public: calls for tenders from public buyers, read from
TED (EU, IT, data and R&D codes
together with your terms), Contracts Finder
(UK) and PNCP (Brazil).
Private: companies hiring contractors. PULSE reads the public job
boards of the companies the check-up found (its leads, partners and
competitors) on Greenhouse,
Lever and
Ashby, then
the job boards Jobicy and
Himalayas, which rank below. Each item says
Direct or Via agency: via agency when the company's name says it is
a staffing or recruiting firm, or the posting says it is written for a
client.
All: both, with the same role from two sources listed once. The
filter also offers Direct and Via agency on their own.

Each item shows its buyer or company, its segment, its contract type and
duration, the value or rate as published (or "not published"), its closing
date, its relevance score and the terms it matched, and a link to its source.
The score adds each matched term's weight, twice when the term is in the
title, plus 0.5 for a tender filed under an IT, data or R&D code. Items that
match no term or score under 1 are not listed; the header says how many, and
how many permanent roles and duplicates were left out. Nothing is stored: the
list is read when you open Leads.
If PULSE knows no expertise yet, the header says why and asks you to name it
in Tune or run the check-up again. If a segment has nothing, it lists the
terms searched, each source checked with what it returned, and the next step.
The sources PULSE checked and does not read (for example SAM.gov, which needs
a key, and Hacker News, whose terms forbid automated reading) are listed with
the reason.
Calls
Call on a lead opens the AI call. It is refused, with every reason listed,
unless your administrator has turned AI calls on and the lead gave consent;
see AI calls to leads. A lead can also be put on
the do-not-call list from its AI call sheet.

Warning: Cold calling and cold email are regulated where you and your leads are:
consent, calling hours, do-not-call lists, and unsubscribe rules. Check the
rules that apply to you before you contact real people.

docs/user-guide/outreach-sequences/.title: Outreach sequences
docs/user-guide/outreach-sequences/.body:
Outreach sequences

An outreach sequence takes one lead from the first touch to a booked
meeting: a cold email, timed follow-ups, call tasks and a LinkedIn touch as a
task. Start one from the lead's card on Leads.
Status: built. Sending needs your own connected mailbox and your
administrator's email switches, which are off by default.
What PULSE does, and what you approve

Nothing is sent without your approval. Every email is a draft until you
approve it: step by step, or the rest of the sequence after the first
approval, as you choose.
Emails go from your own mailbox (see
Email from your own mailbox).
Every email carries your name or company, a postal address and a one-click
unsubscribe link, added by PULSE. An email missing one is refused.
Sends keep your mailbox's daily limit and the lead's working hours (no
weekends, no nights).
Only business addresses found legitimately (the business's own site or form,
your CRM, a published notice) are sequenced.

When a sequence stops
A sequence stops by itself on a reply, a bounce, an unsubscribe or
a booked meeting. An unsubscribe goes on your suppression list and stops
every sequence to that address. You can pause a sequence at any time.
Call steps
A call step is a task for you, with talking points drafted from the lead and
your check-up. With AI calls switched on for your account, it can instead
become an AI call that you approve plan by plan. See
Cold and follow-up calls from Leads.
Meetings
A lead moves to Replied when they answer, and to Meeting proposed when
a time was put to them. Only you set Meeting booked, with Confirm the
meeting or by moving the lead yourself.
Re-engage a quiet lead
A lead you wrote to that never replied can get one short follow-up, without
you hunting for it. Open Content › Automations and choose Re-engage a quiet
lead, then switch it on. It is off until you do.

Switching it on installs an automation of the same name, not armed. You
arm it like any automation, and you can run it as a dry run first.
Each morning it looks at the leads in stage Contacted that never replied. For
each lead whose last email from PULSE is at least your quiet period old
(14 days unless you change it, 3 to 90), it writes one draft in the
lead's sequence. The draft is a short fixed message in your language with the
lead's first name. It never uses what the lead wrote.
Nothing is sent until you approve the draft. After your tap the email goes
out like every sequence email: inside your working hours and daily cap, with
your name, postal address and one-click unsubscribe link, and only if the
address is not on your suppression list.
A lead is never re-engaged twice more: at most 2 follow-ups per lead, ever,
counted from its sequences, and at most 10 drafts a day. A lead that replied,
unsubscribed, is not a business address or already has a sequence running is
left alone, and the run says why.
A reply, a bounce or an unsubscribe stops the draft, like any sequence.

docs/user-guide/email-from-your-mailbox/.title: Email from your mailbox
docs/user-guide/email-from-your-mailbox/.body:
Email from your own mailbox

PULSE sends email from your own mailbox: Gmail, Microsoft 365, or any
mailbox you reach by SMTP. It has no shared sender and never reads your inbox
beyond the replies to emails it sent.
Status: built. Sending is off until your administrator arms the email
switch, and Gmail or Microsoft 365 can be connected only once your
administrator has set up the organisation's sign-in app for it.
Connect your mailbox
Open Settings › Integrations › Email:

Connect Gmail or Connect Microsoft 365 opens the provider's consent
page. If the card says the provider "is not set up on this instance", your
administrator must configure it first.
Set up SMTP asks for your server, port, username, password and from
address. It needs no administrator setup.

Test checks the mailbox without sending anything. The card names the
address PULSE sends from.
Send
On a lead's email draft, Send sends it from your mailbox. Send is offered
only when you are an editor or admin, your administrator has armed sending, a
mailbox is connected and you are under the daily limit (50 emails a day unless
your administrator set another). Otherwise the sheet says which one is
missing and keeps Copy and Open in email.
The name your emails are signed with
Outreach emails, meeting proposals, review requests and call plans are signed
with the name you saved in Outreach settings. If you saved none, PULSE
uses a company name it finds for your account, and the settings say so. Save
your own name to replace it. If no name can be found at all, PULSE refuses to send rather than
sign with a blank.
Replies
PULSE checks for answers to the emails it sent and marks the lead replied,
with the first words of the answer. A Gmail or Microsoft 365 mailbox connected
without the reading permission asks you to Reconnect. Replies to emails
sent through SMTP are not tracked: check your inbox.
Administrators: see Email.

docs/user-guide/ai-calls/.title: AI calls to leads
docs/user-guide/ai-calls/.body:
AI calls to leads

An AI call is a phone call to one lead in which an AI assistant talks to
the lead for you. It follows the lead's drafted call script, works toward the
goal you pick, and writes the outcome, a short summary and the next step to
the lead when the call ends. It also creates a follow-up task.

Warning: Off by default. AI calls stay off until an administrator arms three
switches, and your account switches them on in Settings › Integrations › AI
calls. No call is placed without a person: you tap Call, or you approve
that call's plan in an outreach sequence. Every call opens by saying it is an
AI.

Choose Call on a lead's card, or AI call on its call-script draft. A
call step in an outreach sequence or an
automation places the same call once a person has approved its plan.
What the call says

A statement that it is an automated AI assistant from your company, first, in the call's language.
Who it is calling on behalf of, and a notice about the call.
The drafted script, then the conversation.

If the lead says stop, do not call (or the same in French, Spanish or
Portuguese), the assistant says goodbye, the number goes on your
do-not-call list, and the call is marked Declined.
When PULSE refuses to call
PULSE checks every call and refuses, listing the reasons, for example when:

an administrator has not armed AI calls (PULSE_APPLY_ENABLED,
PULSE_OUTBOUND_CALLS and PULSE_AI_CALLS, see
Switches);
you are a viewer (AI calls need an editor or administrator);
there is no record of the lead's consent to AI calls. Record how the
lead agreed, where the evidence is, and when;
the number is on the do-not-call list;
it is outside the allowed calling hours for the lead;
the lead has had too many AI calls recently, or a call to them is still in
progress;
the lead has no drafted call script, Twilio has no caller number, or speech
is not configured.

Check runs the same checks without calling.
Outcomes



Outcome
Follow-up task




Meeting requested
The next step the summary proposes


Connected
The next step the summary proposes


Voicemail
A call-back task. With leave a short message, the assistant leaves one after the beep, opening with the AI statement first


No answer
A task to try again


Declined
None: the number is on the do-not-call list


Failed
None



The transcript is stored encrypted with the call. Only editors and
administrators can read it. It is never written to the server log.
Calls that come from an outreach sequence are planned and approved first: see
Cold and follow-up calls from Leads.

docs/user-guide/cold-calls-from-sequence.title: Cold and follow-up calls from Leads
docs/user-guide/cold-calls-from-sequence.body:
Cold and follow-up calls from Leads

An outreach sequence has a call step. With AI calls
switched on for your account, that step can become a real AI call: PULSE drafts
a call plan, you read it on an approval card, and the call is placed
only after you approve that exact plan. AI calls are off until an
administrator turns them on (Settings › Integrations › AI calls); with them
off, the call step stays a task for you, as before.
The plan
When a call step falls due, PULSE drafts a plan for that call. The
approval card shows the plan for you to read. Every call opens with the AI statement ("This is an automated AI assistant from your company").
Approving
The plan appears on the lead's card (Leads, History), with where each line
comes from. Approve this plan and call sends the plan you read: if it
changed in between, PULSE refuses. A sequence's "approve the rest" never covers a
call: every call has its own plan and its own approval, and an approval
lapses after a time set by your administrator. Withdraw
cancels the plan. The assistant can draft a plan too (plan the call to
Dana); it only drafts, and you approve on the card.
Approving does not force the call. PULSE still checks, unchanged, the lead's
consent, the allowed calling hours, your do-not-call list and your daily
