why. It never shows zero. This is the same measure as the Response time card
in Leads › Inbound.
Under it, the number of messages still without a first response. If you set a
number of hours in Settings › Account › First response to website enquiries, only
those that have waited longer than that count; for the mailbox and Instagram
channels it counts what is waiting for a person.
Replies to your outreach have no first-response clock, so they are listed but not
timed.
What is counted but not listed
When inbox reading judges that a message is not a vendor pitch, or comes from a
customer or a lead, PULSE leaves it to the other parts of the app and keeps no
record of it. The Inbox shows those only as counts, under Read and counted, not
listed.
Why a line says nothing is read
The top of the screen says, from what PULSE recorded:

when inbox reading is off (it is off until you switch it on in Settings ›
Account), and that nothing in your mailbox is read until then;
when inbox reading works with Gmail only and your mailbox is another provider;
when first response or answering vendor pitches is off.

Related

Answer vendor pitches
First response to enquiries
Leads
Measured, never made up

docs/user-guide/youtube-and-instagram-en.title: Comments on YouTube and Instagram
docs/user-guide/youtube-and-instagram-en.body:
Comments on YouTube and Instagram

Runink PULSE reads the comments on the posts it sent for you on YouTube and
Instagram, drafts an answer to each, and keeps every answer in Campaigns ›
Approvals until a person sends it. This page says what it covers, what it
suggests on other people's videos, and what Instagram and YouTube do not allow
at all.
Comments on your own posts

PULSE looks back 14 days by default (your administrator can set 1 to 60)
at the posts it sent, and reads every page of comments inside that time, up to
a limit per post, newest first.
Each comment gets a drafted reply for you to edit and send. Auto-reply stays
off unless you turn it on, and only for thanks, answers taken from your
approved FAQ and links to your own site.
A reply, like everything PULSE sends, goes through your switches, My
rules and the conscience check. If a check holds it, it stays in Approvals
with the reason and a link to What was checked.
If a platform refuses a permission, the app says Reconnect to allow … and
names the permission, the same way on both platforms.
Spam. A comment that carries a link that is not yours together with an
offer, or three or more links, is not answered: it is proposed to you as
Hide the comment. Nothing is hidden until you approve. On Instagram you
can show the comment again in the app; on YouTube a hidden comment cannot be
restored from PULSE, and the proposal says so.

What PULSE reads besides comments



Platform
Mentions
Direct messages




Instagram
Posts that tag your account (read from your account's tags). Mentions in a caption and story mentions are not read: Instagram only sends them to a server that listens for them, and PULSE does not run one.
Read, and answered only within Instagram's 24 hours after the person's last message. Story replies are not read.


YouTube
Not available: YouTube's interface offers no mentions.
Not available: it offers no direct messages.



The app says "not available" or "not read yet" for these; it never shows an
empty list as if nothing had come.
Suggested comments on other people's YouTube videos
You can switch on Suggest comments on other people's videos under Settings ›
Account. It is off until you do, and your administrator must also have
allowed it.

PULSE picks a video that Brand Analysis › What people are talking about already found for your market, reads its public
title, and drafts one short, useful comment: a question the video left
open, a point it agrees or disagrees with, or a fact you gave PULSE. When it
has nothing true to add it says nothing.
A comment never contains a link, never promotes you, a channel, a code or an
offer, never claims you did something you did not say you did, never uses a
figure the video or your facts do not contain, and never speaks as the
creator or as YouTube.
It waits in Approvals as Suggested comment on …'s video. Nothing is
posted until you approve it, and there is no setting that makes PULSE post
one by itself. You can edit it first; the same rules are checked again.
It is posted as your own YouTube channel: your channel's name stands under
it.
There is a daily limit (3 by default), a pause on a channel after a
suggestion on one of its videos (14 days by default), and a budget of what
PULSE may use of YouTube's daily allowance. A comment held by one of them
stays in Approvals and says why.

Instagram: no comments on other people's posts
Instagram does not allow apps to comment on other accounts' posts. PULSE cannot
and does not do it. Instead, Approvals has Draft an Instagram comment to post
by hand: you paste the post's link and its text, PULSE drafts a comment, and
you copy it and post it yourself in Instagram. There is no send button.
What is not covered
LinkedIn is not part of this. Story mentions and story replies on Instagram are
not read. YouTube community posts, channel mentions and direct messages are not
available through YouTube's interface.

docs/user-guide/results-and-reports/.title: Results and reports
docs/user-guide/results-and-reports/.body:
Results and reports

PULSE shows a result only when something measured it: your own records (what
PULSE did), a platform that reported it (Instagram, LinkedIn, YouTube), or an
account you connected (Google Analytics, Google Ads, Search Console). Anything
else reads Not measured, never 0 and never an estimate. See
Measured and not measured.
Where to find your results



What
Where




The key numbers, with their change
Brand Analysis, for 7, 30 or 90 days


What PULSE did, and this week's results of your posts
Brand Analysis → What PULSE did


Lines over time
Brand Analysis → How you are doing over time


Your measured figures and their impact
The Results card on Brand Analysis


Google searches: clicks, positions, pages losing clicks
Can people find you? (needs Search Console)


A campaign's results against its targets
The campaign's own page, under Results


What happened to one post
Its step trail


Deal values and won revenue
The strip on Leads


Progress on your 30-day plan
Your plan, from your weekly check-ins



Email me this, in What PULSE did, sends you the week's summary from
your own connected mailbox.
What fills them



Source
What it gives
Set up




PULSE's own records
Posts sent, drafts approved, outreach drafted, tasks done, leads moved on. A 0 here is a real 0.
Nothing


Instagram, LinkedIn, YouTube
Each post's results the platform reports (reach, views, reactions, comments, saves, shares, where that kind of post reports them)
Connect the account; see Integrations


Google Analytics
Visits and page views
Connect GA4


Google Ads
Ad views, clicks and spend
Connect Google Ads


Google Search Console
Search clicks, appearances, positions
Connect Search Console


Your weekly check-ins
Followers, posts, engagement, leads, satisfaction
Fill them in on Leads → To do today



Reports
Make a report in Studio → Long reads and audio → Report:

Timeframe, for example Last 30 Days or Q1 2025. Left empty, it is
the last 30 days. A period that reaches past today ends today.
Highlight metrics (optional), separated by commas.
File to download: PDF Document or CSV / Spreadsheet Data.

PULSE first reads your measured records for the period (metrics, the results
of your posts, won revenue) and writes the figures itself. The model is given
only those figures, to write the reading around them, and any sentence naming
a figure that is not in your records is removed. Each source is one of three
things: measured (its figures in a table), not measured, or unreadable
with the reason. A metric you asked to highlight that nothing measured is
listed as not measured. If nothing at all was measured, the model is not
asked to write.
The PDF has a title page with your account and the period, the reading, the
measured figures as tables, and what was not measured. It is laid out in your
language (English, Spanish, French or Portuguese) with that language's number
format, with every accented letter, curly quote, dash and the euro sign drawn
as written. The names of the figures, their notes and the reasons a source
was not measured are in that language too, from PULSE's own word list (the
model does not translate them). Some words are shown as written and labelled
so: the reading (written by the model), a metric you typed to highlight, and
an error recorded while reading a source. A figure PULSE has no word for yet
is shown by its name in the data, never left blank. The CSV keeps the English
names, so a spreadsheet reads the same in every language. The finished
file is also kept in My Library.
The diagnostic's PDF export is laid out the same way; its sections are written
by the model during the audit and shown as written.
Guides, study guides, mind maps, timelines and comparison tables made in
Studio are PDFs too.

docs/user-guide/voice-over-studio/.title: Voice-over studio
docs/user-guide/voice-over-studio/.body:
Voice-over studio

The Voice-over studio turns a script into spoken audio: your own script, or
a piece PULSE wrote for you (a podcast script, a short, an article). The audio
is saved in your library, where you can play it, download it and copy a link.
Every voice-over is spoken by a synthetic voice and is marked
"AI-generated voice", in the app and inside the audio file.
Make one

Open Studio and pick Voice-over, or open a written piece and choose
Make audio, or choose Make audio under a podcast script as it is
written.
Paste or type the script, or use Use a Studio piece. Time codes, stage
directions in brackets and the maker's own lines (such as "Visual:") are not
spoken.
Choose a language (English, French, Spanish or Portuguese) and a
voice. Listen plays a short sample of the voice first.
Choose a pace and, if you like, a title, then Make audio.

A long script is cut into parts, spoken one after the other and joined into one
file; the screen shows which part is being spoken.
You can leave
You can close this screen, or the app: the audio keeps being made on the server
and appears in My voice-overs when it is ready. Each voice-over you ask for is
kept as a job, and My voice-overs lists the ones being made with how far they
are (part 2 of 5), so you can come back to it later.

Stop ends a voice-over you no longer want, and nothing is saved. Closing the
screen never does.
If the voice service did not answer, or the server restarted while the audio was
being made, the job says so with the reason and Try again makes it again from
the start. A job can be tried again up to 3 times, and a retry does not count as a
new voice-over in your daily limit. No half-made audio is ever kept.
The voice service is shared. If it is busy with other accounts, yours shows
Waiting for a free voice slot and starts when it is its turn.

Two voices
Start lines with a name and a colon (Host: and Guest:) and choose a second
voice: each speaker gets their own voice. A script can have at most two
speakers; one with more is refused, with the names it found. With no second
voice chosen, the first voice reads both speakers.
Pace
Pace sets the pauses between sentences and between speakers. It does not
change how fast a voice speaks.
Limits

A script is at most 24,000 characters (about half an hour of speech).
Up to 20 voice-overs a day for each account, one being made at a time. A voice-over
counts when you ask for it, so one that failed or was stopped still counts; trying
it again does not count a second time.
The audio is one WAV file of at most 96 MiB.

When it is not available
If voice output is not set up on your server, or the voice service does not
answer, the screen says so and nothing is made: PULSE never plays a different
voice instead, and never reports audio it did not make. Your own recorded voice is a separate option, switched off unless
allowed: see voice-overs in your own voice.
Your files
Voice-overs are yours alone. Delete removes the audio file. They are part of
the copy of your data you can export and are deleted with your account. A
download link stops working after 24 hours.
The script of a voice-over job is kept sealed only until the audio is ready, or for
3 days when it did not become audio, so you can try again; it is then removed.

docs/user-guide/integrations/.title: Settings → Integrations
docs/user-guide/integrations/.body:
Connect your accounts

Settings → Integrations (/settings?tab=integrations) is one grid of
cards, one per account or channel, in two sections:

Publish to: Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, Website, Website repository,
Podcast, Audiobook, and Email (your mailbox).
Measure & CRM: Google Analytics, Google Ads, Google Search Console,
HubSpot, SAM.gov, and the Website form.

Below the grid is Autopilot (see
Autopilot and agencies).
This page is the owner's side: what you click and what you get. Some
connections first need your administrator to register PULSE with the platform
(an app in Meta's, Google's or LinkedIn's developer console). When that is
missing, the card says so and names what the administrator must set. The
administrator's side is in Connections and
Switches and arming order.
PULSE keeps every token and password encrypted, and never shows a pasted one
again.
What a "Publish to" card tells you

Active: your switch. An Active channel gets PULSE's daily drafts, is
planned in your campaigns, and may publish. Turning it off stops all three.
Save after changing it.
A one-line status: Ready to publish, or Can't publish: and the
reason in plain words, for example Connect an account first.,
Publishing is switched off for this whole deployment. Posts are kept and
marked held back., or Only this deployment's named publishers can post
here.
Recent dispatches: what was posted, held back or failed, with the date.

Instagram, YouTube and LinkedIn
Connect opens the platform's own sign-in in a new browser tab. Sign in,
allow what PULSE asks for, then come back. (If nothing opens, allow pop-ups
for PULSE.)
Once connected, the card shows:

Signed in, and when the sign-in ends. PULSE renews this sign-in before
it ends where the platform allows it; otherwise it says Reconnect before
that date. A failed renewal is shown with its date and reason.
What each feature has: Publishing, Results, Comments and Direct
messages, each allowed, needs a named permission, not checked,
or not offered by that platform to apps (YouTube has no mentions and no
direct messages for apps).
Reconnect asks the platform again, for example to allow a permission you
declined. Disconnect removes PULSE's access at the platform where it can
and deletes the stored sign-in; your settings for the account are kept.

If your administrator has not set up sign-in for a platform, the card says
… sign-in isn't set up on this server and offers to paste a token
instead. A pasted token works, but PULSE can neither check its permissions
nor renew it, and the card says so.



Platform
What you connect
What PULSE does with it




Instagram
A professional (business or creator) Instagram account linked to a Facebook Page, through Facebook Login
Publishes posts, carousels, Reels and Stories; reads results, comments, mentions and direct messages for Autopilot


YouTube
Your Google account and its YouTube channel
Uploads YouTube Shorts; reads views, likes, comments and watch time


LinkedIn
Your LinkedIn member account
Posts as you. Connect company pages (when your administrator has enabled it) lets you choose a company page you administer as the author instead



Google Search Console
Connect Search Console signs in with Google, read-only: PULSE never changes
anything in Search Console. Then Choose the site PULSE reads; the one that
matches the site you audited is marked. PULSE reads it once a day: the clicks,
appearances, click rate and position of each search, for the last 28 days and
the 28 before (Google's figures run about two days behind).
The card says when it last read and up to which day, or why the last read
failed. Read now, Change site and Disconnect are on it. If your
Google account has no verified site, add your site at
search.google.com/search-console first, then reconnect.
What it fills: Can people find you? on Brand Analysis, the Search
clicks and Search impressions lines, and the demand behind content ideas
and campaign plans ("people searched X; your site ranks 11").
Google Analytics and Google Ads
These are connected with a key you create in Google Cloud and paste on the
card:

Google Analytics: the JSON key of a service account with access to your
GA4 property, and the numeric Property ID (GA4 Admin → Property Settings).
Google Ads: the JSON key of a service account with domain-wide
delegation, your Ads Customer ID, a Developer Token, optionally a Login
Customer ID (manager account), and the user email to act as.

Test Connection checks them. They fill the visits, page views, ad views,
ad clicks and spend on Brand Analysis and in reports. If this is not something
you do yourself, ask whoever manages your Google Cloud; the details are in
Connections.
Your website
There are two cards, for two jobs:

Website publishes your approved blog articles to your site through
GitHub. Paste a GitHub token that can push to your site's repository. Which
repository it publishes to is set by your administrator.
Website repository is where PULSE proposes fixes to your site as pull
requests. See below.

Website repository
Fill in the Owner (your GitHub user or organization), the Repository
name, the Base branch, and a Fine-grained access token: create it on
GitHub under Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens, for this one
repository only, with Contents and Pull requests set to Read and write.
Then Connect and check. The card says Connected, or what is wrong:
Missing permission, Token rejected, Base branch not found or
GitHub unreachable. Check again re-checks it.
From then on, a fix the site score found can be proposed with Propose as
pull request on the site-score report. PULSE writes
the change on a new branch and opens a pull request for you to review and
merge. PULSE never merges and never changes your base branch. Each fix
shows its pull request's state as last read from GitHub: Pull request
open, Merged or Closed without merging, or No pull request needed,
or Withheld by the plan gate when PULSE's reviewer did not agree with the
change.
Proposing needs an administrator account, and your administrator must have
switched on publishing and site fixes on this PULSE. Until then the button is
refused with the reason.
Podcast and audiobook
Nothing to connect: PULSE publishes these itself, in its own podcast feed that
Spotify and Apple read. Turn them Active to use them.
Email
Connect your own mailbox, so that Send on a lead's email sends from your
address: Connect Gmail, Connect Microsoft 365, or an SMTP server. With
Gmail or Microsoft 365, PULSE also sees who replied. See
Leads → Email.
HubSpot
Paste the access token of a HubSpot Private App (in HubSpot: Settings →
Integrations → Private Apps) with the CRM contacts permissions. Then Sync
from HubSpot on Leads imports your contacts, new leads PULSE finds are added
to HubSpot, and your website form's enquiries go there too.
SAM.gov
For US federal tenders on Leads:
paste your SAM.gov public API key (on sam.gov: your profile, Account Details,
API key). PULSE only reads tenders with it.
Website form
Turns your site's contact form into leads. See
Website form.

docs/user-guide/voice-over-own-voice/.title: Voice-overs in your own voice
docs/user-guide/voice-over-own-voice/.body:
Voice-overs in your own voice

By default a voice-over is spoken by one of the platform's built-in voices.
Voice-overs in your own voice is a separate option that is switched off
until you, your administrator and the voice service have each allowed it. The
voice is your own, made from the recording you added with your consent in
Digital twins: nothing else can be uploaded here,
and no other person's voice is accepted anywhere.
What has to be on

Your administrator has switched on PULSE_OWN_VOICE for the server.
The voice service has recorded voices turned on. This is a setting of the
platform's voice service, off by default, and it uses more memory and the
server's graphics card. If it is off, the option reads Not available on
this server.
You have switched on Settings > Account > My own voice.
You have a recording of your own voice with a recorded consent, and the
consent has not been withdrawn.

Make one
In the Voice-over studio, the My own voice card shows under the voice
choices when it is switched on. Choose Use my own voice, then tick the
confirmation each time: "This voice is yours. You confirm you are the
speaker." Only a count of confirmations is kept, never your words. Then choose
Make in my voice.
Limits

A script in your own voice is at most 3,000 characters, because making a
voice from a recording is slow and uses the server's graphics card.
Up to 5 voice-overs a day in your own voice (PULSE_OWN_VOICE_DAILY_CAP).
They also count toward the 20 voice-overs a day of the studio.
One at a time for each account.
A script that speaks as another real person, that tries to persuade on
politics, or that gives medical or legal advice or claims is refused with a
reason, and the refused text is not kept.
Your own voice is never used for phone calls.

What it is called
The audio is a synthetic voice made from your recording. It is marked
"AI-generated voice (your voice)" on the screen, and the file carries
"AI-generated voice" and "voice: own (synthetic)". PULSE does not add a
watermark, and does not say the voice cannot be told from yours.
Your recording and withdrawing
Your recording stays sealed in your own storage. For each voice-over PULSE
gives it to the voice service for that one job and asks the service to forget
the voice when the job ends, whether it worked, failed or was stopped.
Withdrawing the consent for the recording, deleting the recording or the
twin, or deleting your account stops a voice-over being made and deletes the
voice-overs made in that voice, with their audio files, the same way the
videos made from your recordings are deleted. The confirmation says so.
Voice-overs made with a built-in voice are not touched.

docs/user-guide/assistant-and-voice/.title: Assistant and voice
docs/user-guide/assistant-and-voice/.body:
Assistant and voice

The assistant
The assistant floats over every screen, and it is told which screen you are on.
It sends your messages to ModelService.Complete with the assistant agent and
streams the answer back.
Everything it says comes from the platform's own model. Nothing goes to an
outside AI service.
Ask it to audit a site
One line with a verb and a web address — Audit example.com — starts the
whole audit: PULSE reads the site, scores it, writes the diagnosis, and fills
the pages that act on it, stage by stage. The verbs it recognizes are audit,
analyse (or analyze), scan, review, inspect, and score.
A line with a question mark is treated as a question instead. See
Audit a domain.
A web address whose host is not a domain runs the site relevance audit on its
own and opens the full report.
Ask about your data, and let it propose actions
The assistant can read your own PULSE records to answer: your leads (by
stage) and one lead's details, your latest audit and its findings, your
metrics (when nothing has been measured yet it says so instead of giving 0),
content waiting for your approval, your campaigns, and follow-up tasks that
are due. While it reads, the chat shows what it is doing ("Reading your
leads…"). Each read is also listed on your activity card.
It can also propose an action: start an audit, find leads, draft outreach for
a lead, move a lead's stage, create a campaign draft, write a Studio
whitepaper or presentation outline, approve or schedule a content item. A
proposal appears as a card that says what it will do and on which page.
Nothing runs until you tap Confirm. Confirm is checked again on the
server: your role must still allow the action, and the card's details cannot
be changed from the app.
The assistant never sends an email, posts or calls by itself. Approving or
scheduling a content item goes through the same publishing switches as the
Campaigns board's own buttons.
Every read and every action is done with your account: the assistant cannot
do anything you could not do by tapping.
A figure it cannot find in your data
When the assistant tells you a figure about your own results (for example
"you got 40 leads this month"), PULSE checks that figure against the data the
assistant was given for that answer: your account, the page or search it read,
what you attached and said, and what its reads returned. A sentence whose
figure is not in that data is not shown. In its place the assistant says, once,
that it cannot see that figure in the data it was given, in your language (English,
French, Spanish or Portuguese). The rest of the answer is shown as written.
Advice and general statements are never changed. This is a check against
invented figures, not a proof that every claim is right, and there is no
setting for it.
Talk instead of typing

Voice input. The microphone records what you say and turns it into text on the platform's own servers. Where a deployment has not set this up, the app says it is unavailable.
Spoken replies. The assistant can read answers aloud through
ModelService.SynthesizeSpeech, on the platform's own servers. Where a
deployment has turned voice output off, the reply stays text. A custom voice
does not speak live; a stock voice of the same language reads instead, and
the panel says so.

Voice requires you to be signed in.
Commands go through the assistant
The assistant is the only place you type or speak a command (there is no
separate command bar). It understands these in English, French, Spanish and
Portuguese, whatever language the app is set to. Each command and its answer
go in the conversation and in your chat history like any other message.



Command
Examples
What happens




Audit a site
audit rosasbakery.com, audite rosasbakery.com, audita rosasbakery.com, analisa rosasbakery.com
Starts the audit and opens Brand Analysis on it


Read the verdict
read, read the verdict, lis le verdict, lee el veredicto, lê o veredito
Writes the last audit's verdict (the first thing to fix, and what it was based on) and reads it aloud, whether or not spoken replies are on


Send it to a contact
notify Ana, préviens Ana, avisa a Ana, envia para a Ana
Opens the same Send / Call window Leads uses, with Ana and WhatsApp chosen, and the verdict as the message


Call a contact
call Ana, appelle Ana, llama a Ana, liga para a Ana
The same window, with a call chosen


Open a page
open leads, ouvre les campagnes, abre el estudio, abre o histórico de conversas
Opens Brand Analysis, Leads, Tenders, Campaigns, Studio, Settings, or a Settings tab (Account, Integrations, Clients, Subscription, Chat history)



Send and Call only reach a contact an admin configured. If no contact matches
the name, the assistant says so and lists the ones it can reach. Nothing is
sent or dialled until you check the preview and press Send now or
Call now; the assistant then says what became of it. See
Telephony and messaging.
A line with a question mark is always a question, never a command.
Voice calls with the assistant
The full-screen call view (/call) lets you talk with the assistant. Where a deployment has not set up voice calls, the app says so.
Phone calls to leads are different. See
AI calls to leads.

docs/user-guide/questions-from-pulse/.title: Questions from PULSE
docs/user-guide/questions-from-pulse/.body:
Questions from PULSE

Sometimes the assistant or an agent cannot answer from your own data (the
check-up, your leads and your plan have nothing on it). It may then ask the
account's owner one short question instead of guessing.
Status: built. Questions always appear in the app. Sending them to your
phone is off by default.
Where questions appear
A question appears in the bell and in Settings › Account, with when it
was asked. Answer it there, or dismiss it. Your answer is used only for that
one question. An unanswered question expires.
When the assistant wants to ask, it shows a card first so you can confirm,
unless nothing would leave the app.
Questions on your phone
You can also get questions by SMS or WhatsApp on a number you picked
yourself. This is off until you switch it on in Settings › Account,
and it also needs your administrator to have set up messaging and armed the
send switches. Even then PULSE respects the quiet hours you choose. Reply to the message to answer. Reply STOP to switch it off.
PULSE never phones you to ask a question. Administrators: see
Agents that reach the user.

docs/user-guide/tools/.title: AI tools
docs/user-guide/tools/.body:
The AI tools and their model cards

Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine does its AI work through a small set
of agents. Each one has its own
instructions, its own limits, and its own guardrails, but they all run on the
same model server. A model card says, in plain language, what one agent does,
what it reads, what it produces, who checks its work, and where it stops.
The cards



Agent
What you meet it as
Status




Diagnostic analyst
The written diagnosis from a check-up, and the metrics read-out
Built


Market research
Market and trend research, competitor channels, and guest spots
Built


Strategy planner
Recalculating the route of a 30-day follow-up cycle
Retired: replaced by the 90-day plan


Channel content creator
Posts, emails, outreach drafts, and the shorter Studio pieces
Built; publishing off until armed


Long-form studio
Whitepapers, blog posts, and the weekly audiobook
Built; publishing off until armed


Partnership outreach
First-contact messages to podcasts, channels, and brands
Built; sends nothing without approval and an armed channel


Sales and voice agent
Cold-call scripts, live replies on a phone call, and churn watch
Built; AI calls off by default


Content strategy and roadmaps
Content pillars and phased roadmaps
Built


PULSE assistant
The chat on every screen
Built


Self-healing operations agent
Keeps PULSE's own services running; the one agent that acts automatically, with an off switch
Built



What every agent has in common
The model. Every request goes to the platform's own models, on the
platform's own inference servers. An agent's own configuration sets its
instructions, never its weights. No plan routes to a different or "smarter"
model. See Sovereign inference.
Where it runs. On the deployment's own inference server. PULSE calls no
outside AI service. Some agents read the public web or your connected accounts while
they work, and PULSE talks to the services you connect (HubSpot, LinkedIn,
Google Analytics and others) as described in
Connections.
Text in, text out. The agents read and write text. No agent creates images on its own:
a still image is made only when a person asks for one with Create image in Studio, and it
stays a labelled "AI-generated" draft until a person approves it. Carousel slides and the frames of the Reels
and Stories PULSE makes are made by PULSE itself from the agent's text,
and videos are assembled by PULSE, with speech from the platform's speech service. See
Studio.
Grounded, or honest about not being. An agent that makes claims works from real material, and says so when it has none.
Guardrails before the model. Before any agent is called, PULSE checks the
request against a shared set of safety rules and refuses what they do not
allow. Each agent's card describes the commitments it keeps.
Outside text is data, not instructions. Web pages, search results,
attached sources, lead and CRM records, inbound customer messages, and call
transcripts reach an agent as material to read, never as instructions to
follow.
Value first. Every agent that writes for an audience follows the same
brand rule: teach the reader something useful, mention your product at most
once and only as an honest example, no hype words, no fake urgency, and end
with a real question rather than a hard sell.
People decide. Agents draft, recommend, and score. (The
self-healing operations agent is the exception for
PULSE's own infrastructure: it applies a fixed list of safe actions
automatically, and an operator can turn that off.) Drafts go to Drafts to
approve on Campaigns. A post is published only when a person approved
that piece and an administrator armed the channel; rejecting a piece
withholds its scheduled posts. Two things can reply without a person: answers to inbound WhatsApp or SMS
messages from a known contact, off unless an administrator sets
PULSE_WHATSAPP_AUTOREPLY, and Autopilot's answers to three kinds of simple
comments, off unless the account turns them on. Both pass the same
guardrails, and both still need the channel armed. See Publishing controls.
Some proposals also pass through the plan gate,
and the agent activity card shows every run
as it happens.

docs/user-guide/tools/diagnostic-analyst.title: Diagnostic analyst
docs/user-guide/tools/diagnostic-analyst.body:
Diagnostic analyst

Status: Built. It runs every check-up on the platform's own models.
What it does
Give it a website and your social accounts, and it writes a diagnosis of where
your marketing stands and what to do in the next 30 days.

Writes the diagnosis behind every check-up:
brand overview, positioning, SWOT, channel recommendations, content
strategy, competitive landscape, search intent and campaign ideas, and a
strategic opinion. Search intent and campaign ideas are shown at the end of
the channel recommendations.
Prescribes a role, priority, content ideas, and KPIs for each channel, and
recommends long-form formats.
Lays out the 4-week plan (the cronogram) that seeds your first follow-up
cycle.
Reads your metrics summary for a date range and writes a short read-out:
summary, insights, recommendations, and its confidence.
Writes the diagnosis stage of the one-phrase
Audit  run, which produces the
same analysis from a domain name alone.

What it reads

The pages of your website, read live when the audit runs. The audit stops if
the site cannot be read.
The LinkedIn URL, Instagram handle, and goals you enter in the audit form.
Public web research about your niche and competitors.
Your business profile, and Google Analytics or Google Ads signals when those
are connected.
For the metrics read-out: the follower, impression, engagement, click, lead,
and conversion figures PULSE has synced.

What it produces
A structured diagnosis, saved with the sources it used. PULSE then copies its findings into the rest of the app: draft
content, a draft campaign, a follow-up cycle, audience profiles, and a market
summary. See Audit a domain.
A diagnosis has a time limit. A phase that does not finish is named on the card, and the run ends with a partial result, shown as the partial answer it is, never as a finished analysis.
Human oversight

The diagnosis is advice. You read it and decide what to act on.
The drafts it seeds wait in Drafts to approve on Campaigns, and the campaign it
seeds is a draft. The 4-week plan queues scheduled posts only for channels an
administrator has already armed, and a queued post goes out only after you
approve its content. For a disarmed channel nothing is queued at all — the
task stays in Your plan and its draft in Drafts to approve.
Channel prescriptions and brand-visibility insights can be withheld by the
plan gate when the judge disagrees
with them. A withheld prescription never becomes a draft.
It cannot publish, move budget, or change a campaign.

Model
The deployment's base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink
Server, our own open-source model with no third-party AI service. See
Sovereign inference.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own inference server: Runink's shared machines on
a Trial, your own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside
AI service is used on any plan.
Reading your website and researching your niche means PULSE fetches public
web pages while the audit runs.
Guardrails

Never invents market or competitor figures. PULSE refuses requests to
fabricate them.
No targeting or analysis by protected characteristics.
It recommends; it never publishes or spends.
Your website and web research are read as material, never as instructions.
Follows the shared value-first brand rule and writes in the language you
use.

Getting good results

Give it every channel you want analysed: it works from your website and the
profiles you list in the audit.
Competitor observations come from competitors' public pages.
Its 0–10 channel scores are judgements to guide priorities, not
measurements.

docs/user-guide/tools/market-research/.title: Market research
docs/user-guide/tools/market-research/.body:
Market research

Status: Built. It reads the public web through the shared crawler, which obeys robots.txt.
What it does
The market research agent researches your market and tells you which topics, hashtags, profiles, and
channels are worth your attention.

Researches a topic and niche: trending topics, hashtag clusters, suggested
profiles, a market summary, and competitive intelligence.
Finds competitors' YouTube and Instagram channels.
Finds channels and podcasts where you could appear as a guest.
Runs the research stages of the one-phrase
Audit , in the background after
the diagnosis has already been returned. Nobody waits for it.

See The Brand Analysis pages.
What it reads

Live web search results for your topic, niche, region, and language.
Any extra sources you attach: a search seed, a website or YouTube URL that
PULSE scrapes, or pasted text.
The brand overview from your diagnosis, so its suggestions fit your brand.
Your like and dislike marks on trending posts, which ground later calls.

What it produces
A research result: topics with a 0–1 relevance score, hashtag clusters,
suggested profiles with the reason each is relevant, and content
opportunities. Channel and guest results carry an audience size only when
the search results state one for that channel, a 0–1 fit score, and a
contact hint when one was found. When no figure was found, the audience shows
as unknown.
Everything it finds is saved with its source and the date. Brand Analysis's
market pages then open on what the last run found, read straight from
your own records — no new search, no model call — rather than re-researching
the web every time a page is opened. Guest opportunities also appear under
Partners to contact, scored for relevance to you and never with a follower figure the
search results did not state.
Human oversight

It recommends. You choose what goes into your plan.
It cannot publish, launch a campaign, or contact anyone. Partner messages
are drafted by Partnership outreach and sent by you.

Model
The deployment's base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink
Server, our own open-source model with no third-party AI service. See
Sovereign inference.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own inference server: Runink's shared machines on
a Trial, your own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside
AI service is used on any plan.
Research means PULSE fetches public web pages and search results while it
works.
Guardrails

Refuses to collect private personal data.
Refuses requests to invent engagement, follower, or reach numbers. A
follower or audience figure the model gives is kept only if the search
results state it; otherwise it is shown as unknown, never estimated.
Treats web pages and search results as material to read, never as
instructions.
Research and recommendation only. Requests to publish or run a campaign are
out of its scope.

Reading its results

Audience sizes are copied from the search results, not measured on the
platforms. A channel shows unknown when the results did not state a
figure.
It researches the public web at the time of the search.
Mention counts and trends show attention, not buying intent.

docs/user-guide/tools/strategy-planner/.title: Strategy planner
docs/user-guide/tools/strategy-planner/.body:
Strategy planner


Warning: Retired on 2026-11-06 with the 30-day follow-up cycle: the 90-day plan
replaces both. Its targets are reasoned per business from public
benchmarks, and its weekly review keeps your earlier check-ins.

What it did
It kept your 30-day plan realistic: when you ask, it recalculates the route
from how your weekly check-ins have moved.

Reviews the check-in history of a follow-up cycle week over week.
Says what is working, what to change, and what to drop, and why.
Adjusts the content mix, the effort per channel, and the KPI targets to
your actual trajectory.

The first plan of a cycle comes from the
diagnostic analyst. This agent revises it. See
Your plan.
What it reads

The follow-up cycle and its planner tasks, with their status.
Your weekly check-ins: new followers, posts, engagements, leads,
satisfaction, and your notes on what worked and what did not.
Your latest diagnosis, including its brand overview.

What it produces
A revised plan, shown once it has passed the brand and output checks: weekly themes and goals, daily
tasks with a channel, type, time estimate, and priority, KPI targets with an
optimistic and a conservative figure, and the adjustments it made, each tied
to the check-in numbers that triggered it.
Human oversight

The revised plan is a recommendation. You decide what to change.
It cannot write or publish posts, run a diagnosis, or move budget.

Model
The deployment's base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink
Server, our own open-source model with no third-party AI service. See
Sovereign inference.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own inference server: Runink's shared machines on
a Trial, your own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside
AI service is used on any plan.
Guardrails

Refuses requests to invent KPI results or check-in data. It works from the
numbers you entered.
Will not endorse unsustainable work patterns. Plans include rest days. It
does not know your calendar, so tell it in a check-in note if your time is
limited.
Planning only. Requests to publish or run a diagnosis are out of its scope.
Follows the shared value-first brand rule.

Getting good results

Log your check-ins: each recalculation works from them, so regular
check-ins give a sharper route.
Targets are planning aids, not forecasts.

docs/user-guide/tools/channel-content-cr.title: Channel content creator
docs/user-guide/tools/channel-content-cr.body:
Channel content creator

Status: Built. It drafts only; nothing is published until a person approves the piece and an administrator arms the channel (off by default).
What it does
It turns a brief, a diagnosis, or a campaign into channel-native copy that
teaches the reader something, with your product mentioned at most once.

Writes a post for one channel and topic when you ask
(Studio).
Drafts the daily copy for each active campaign: a LinkedIn post in a row of
its own, and one combined X and Instagram draft. Both are staged for review
and neither is scheduled.
Drafts outreach for a lead: a cold email and a LinkedIn message
(Leads).
Writes the shorter Studio pieces: podcast and
short-video scripts, presentation outlines, infographic copy, and report
drafts, plus course modules.
Drafts the ad copy for a campaign and finds content gaps your audience
wants filled.

What it reads

Your brief: channel, topic, tone, audience, language, and extra context.
The diagnosis you ground it in, especially its brand overview and
positioning.
The day's trending topics, for the daily social drafts.
For lead outreach: the lead's company and what is publicly known about it.

What it produces
Text drafts in the shape each channel expects, for example a LinkedIn post
with a hook before the "see more" cut and a few hashtags, or a TikTok script
with visual and voice-over lines. When a feature asks for a specific format,
that format wins: a lead email is a subject line and the message, and a
LinkedIn message is the message alone, with no hashtags or notes. Where an image belongs, it describes the image in words; it does not
make one.
Human oversight

Content drafts, including the daily campaign drafts and campaign plans, go
to Drafts to approve on Campaigns. You edit, approve, or reject each one.
The daily LinkedIn post is a draft and only a draft. It is never put on a
schedule; once approved, Download on its card gives you the text to paste yourself. A
generation that came back empty, truncated, or as a guard's refusal is
recorded as a failure instead of being stored as a post. A draft over
LinkedIn's 3,000-character limit is still staged, with that said in its
title, so you trim it rather than discover it on paste.
A scheduled post goes out only once you approved its content. Rejecting a
piece withholds its scheduled posts.
Lead outreach drafts are saved on the lead. PULSE does not send them.
Nothing is published until an administrator arms the channel. Approving
alone does not publish to a disarmed channel. See
Publishing controls.
A campaign plan is a proposal: creating a campaign does not activate it.
Content gaps pass through the plan gate.

Model
The deployment's base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink
Server, our own open-source model with no third-party AI service. See
Sovereign inference.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own inference server: Runink's shared machines on
a Trial, your own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside
AI service is used on any plan.
Guardrails

Value first, no hard sell. The reader's problem is the subject. Your
product appears at most once, as an honest example. No hype words, no fake
urgency, and it ends with a real question.
Never invents statistics, studies, or customer results. It uses the figures
in your brief.
Treats lead details, web pages, and search results as material, never as
instructions.
Refuses unsubstantiated or deceptive claims.
Will not request payments or credentials.
Its output is screened before it reaches you, as described in
Sovereign inference.

Getting good results

It writes text. Creatives are covered in
Studio.
It learns your brand from the diagnosis and brief: run a check-up and give
a detailed brief for drafts that sound like you.

Illustrative example
Invented brief and figure.

Brief: audience warehouse supervisors; channel X; figure to use:
"re-slotting the top 50 SKUs monthly cut walking time by 18% in a pilot".
Draft: "Most picking time is walking. Re-slotting your top 50 SKUs every
month cut walking time by 18% in one pilot. Which SKUs moved most on your
floor last month? #warehouse #logistics"

docs/user-guide/tools/long-form-studio/.title: Long-form studio
docs/user-guide/tools/long-form-studio/.body:
Long-form studio

Status: Built. It drafts only; publishing to a blog, podcast or audiobook feed is off until an administrator arms it.
What it does
It is PULSE's long-form copywriter: it writes the pieces a specialist reads, or
listens to, to the end.

Writes whitepapers in Studio: an executive
summary, sections that each make one argument, and a conclusion with next
steps.
Writes the blog posts the social engine drafts when the blog channel is
armed.
Writes the weekly audiobook, as prose meant to be read aloud.

Shorter Studio pieces (podcast and short-video scripts, outlines, reports) are
written by the channel content creator.
What it reads

The brief: topic, industry, length, and any instructions you give.
For a whitepaper, the product facts shipped with the deployment.
For the daily blog draft: the campaign's name, objective, and audience, and
that day's web research.

It is deliberately not given your marketing diagnosis. A whitepaper is a
document about a product, and grounding it on a marketing diagnosis turns it
into a channel plan for someone else's business.
What it produces
Long text, shown once it has passed the brand and output checks:
markdown with headings and short paragraphs for written pieces, and plain
flowing prose with no lists or tables for audio. Audio itself is produced by
the platform's text-to-speech, not by this agent.
The length it can write in one pass depends on the deployment's time budget.
See Sovereign inference.
Human oversight

You edit and approve every piece. Saved pieces wait in Drafts to approve
on Campaigns like any other content.
Blog posts, podcast episodes, and the audiobook publish only when an
administrator has armed that channel. See
Publishing controls.

Model
The deployment's base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink
Server, our own open-source model with no third-party AI service. See
Sovereign inference.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own inference server: Runink's shared machines on
a Trial, your own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside
AI service is used on any plan.
Guardrails

Value first, no hard sell. It teaches the topic; your product appears at
most once, as an honest example, never as the headline.
Facts only from the brief and the product facts. Every capability claim has to
trace to a passage it was given. It never invents statistics, studies,
quotes, customer names, or case results. If a point needs a number it was
not given, it makes the point without one.
No verified source, said out loud. When there are no product facts on the
topic, the agent writes from the topic and industry alone, rather than inventing capabilities, integrations, certifications,
customers, or partnerships.
No hype words, no clichés, no fake urgency.
Will not handle payments or credentials.
Its output is screened before it reaches you.

Getting good results

It writes from the brief and the product facts, so a detailed brief gives a
richer piece.
Very long documents follow the deployment's time budget; see
Sovereign inference.
It writes text; audio comes from the platform's text-to-speech.

docs/user-guide/tools/partnership-outrea.title: Partnership outreach
docs/user-guide/tools/partnership-outrea.body:
Partnership outreach

Status: Built. It drafts first-contact messages; nothing is sent without a person's approval and an armed channel.
What it does
For a podcast, channel, or brand the market research agent found, it
drafts a short first message proposing a collaboration that clearly helps both
sides, such as a guest-episode swap.
See Leads → Partners.
What it reads

What is known about the partner from the market research: its channel, its
audience, and its angle.
Your diagnosis: your positioning, audience, and offer.

What it produces
A draft in four labelled parts:

Subject: one line.
Value for them: why the collaboration helps their show and audience.
Value for us: why it helps you.
Message: a 120–180 word body ending with one small ask, such as a reply
to schedule a recording.

Human oversight

It only drafts. Each message is saved with status draft. You review
it, edit it, and send it yourself. PULSE sends nothing.

Model
The deployment's base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink
Server, our own open-source model with no third-party AI service. See
Sovereign inference.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own inference server: Runink's shared machines on
a Trial, your own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside
AI service is used on any plan.
Guardrails

Two-sided value first. Every message says what the partner gets, not
only what you want.
No hard sell. No hype, no spammy superlatives, no pressure. The goal of
a first message is a reply, not a deal.
Never invents facts about the partner. When little is known about a
show, it keeps its claims general rather than making up numbers. Requests
to invent audience or download figures are refused.
Draft only. Requests to send, publish, or pay are refused.
The shared input guardrails apply to every request.

Getting good results

It writes from what the market research found, so a fuller partner record gives a more
specific message.
It drafts the message; you send it and follow up on replies.

docs/user-guide/tools/sales-and-voice-ag.title: Sales and voice agent
docs/user-guide/tools/sales-and-voice-ag.body:
Sales and voice agent

Status: Built. Scripts and call plans are drafted for leads; AI calls are off by default and need an administrator to arm them, the account's switch, the lead's recorded consent and a person's approval.
What it does
It is PULSE's sales development persona: it writes cold-call scripts, speaks
short replies on a live phone call, and flags leads at risk of going cold.

Drafts a cold-call script for each lead that Find Leads prospects,
grounded in what it found on that company's own website
(Leads).
On a phone call you place with Call, replies to what the person says, using the lead's cold-call script when one exists.
Once a day, rates synced HubSpot leads as high, medium, or low risk of
stalling, so PULSE can schedule a retention task for the high-risk ones
(Churn watch).

Cold emails and LinkedIn messages for leads are written by the
channel content creator.
What it reads

For a script: the lead's name, title, and company, and, for prospected
leads, gaps found on the lead's website.
For churn watch: the lead's name, company, stage, and notes.
Your diagnosis, to ground the pitch in your positioning.
On a call: what the person says.

What it produces

A short script: an opener, a reason for calling, questions, and one next
step.
On a call: short natural spoken replies, read out by the platform's text-to-speech.
For churn watch: a single risk rating per lead, judged from its stage and notes (not predicted from history).

Human oversight

Every call needs a person's approval. A call is placed from a lead's
Call action, or by an outreach sequence or automation only after a
person approved that call's plan. AI calls are off until an administrator
arms them, and every call opens by saying it is an AI.
During a call, replies are spoken as they are generated. No one approves
each reply before it is heard, so review the lead's script before you call.
Scripts are drafts saved on the lead.
A high-risk rating only creates a retention task in a follow-up cycle. A
person decides what to do with it.

Telephony set-up
A call to a lead is an AI call over the Twilio voice
settings an administrator saves. Each call needs the lead's recorded consent for
that exact number, the allowed calling hours, a number
that is not on the do-not-call list (an unreadable list refuses the call), the
attempt cap, and it opens by saying it is an AI. The earlier Asterisk path is
retired.
Outbound calling is also off by default at the deployment level and has to
be armed deliberately, and only an editor or above can place a call. The full
set-up is in
Telephony and messaging.

Warning: Outbound cold calling is regulated. Consent, calling hours, do-not-call lists,
and recording disclosure are the operator's responsibility.

Model
The deployment's base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink
Server, our own open-source model with no third-party AI service. See
Sovereign inference.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own inference server, with speech-to-text and
text-to-speech on the platform's own speech services: Runink's shared machines
on a Trial, your own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No
outside AI service is used on any plan. The phone call itself travels through
the Twilio account set on the Messaging page.
Guardrails

Lead with their problem, not the pitch. One clear, low-friction next
step. No hype, no fake urgency.
Short and human. Spoken replies are brief, and objections get a brief acknowledgement, never an argument.
No placeholders. It never says "[Name]" or "[company]"; if it does not
know a detail, it talks around it.
Never passes as a person. Requests to claim to be human, or to
impersonate someone, are refused.
Never invents customer results, prices, or statistics, and never takes
payments or card details.
On calls, each reply passes the shared guardrails.

Scope

It works from the lead record, the script, and the call so far.
It speaks and drafts; follow-ups such as booking a meeting are yours.
(Placing a call moves the lead to Talking; that is PULSE's board, not
the agent's decision.)
A risk rating is a judgement from the stage and notes, not a prediction
model.

docs/user-guide/tools/content-strategy-a.title: Content strategy and roadmaps
docs/user-guide/tools/content-strategy-a.body:
Content strategy and roadmaps

Status: Built.
What it does
It turns your diagnosis and real market signals into content pillars and a
roadmap. (It used to write Customer 360 profiles and journey maps; those left
PULSE on 2026-10-26 — audience profiles are a Runink FACE and Runink TIDDE concept.)

Drafts a content strategy: 3–5 weighted content pillars, a posting cadence,
and an alignment score.
Drafts a phased go-to-market roadmap.

What it reads

Your diagnosis, including its audience segments.
Google Analytics and Google Ads figures, when those are connected.
Live search signals for the audience.
The audience and channels you choose.

What it produces
Content pillars whose weights sum to 100, and roadmaps of 3–4 phases, each with a timeframe,
initiatives, and an expected outcome. Some of these come back as structured
data the app displays as cards.
Human oversight

Strategies and roadmaps are planning documents on pages you
control. Nothing is sent to a customer.
Content pillars and roadmap phases pass through the
plan gate, which withholds proposals
its judge disagrees with.
It cannot contact anyone, publish, or launch a campaign.

Model
The deployment's base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink
Server, our own open-source model with no third-party AI service. See
Sovereign inference.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own inference server: Runink's shared machines on
a Trial, your own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside
AI service is used on any plan.
It reads your connected analytics and live search results while it works.
Guardrails

Aggregate segments only. It describes groups, never a real named
person.
No targeting by protected characteristics. It does not infer them, and
PULSE refuses requests to segment, target, or exclude people by them.
Never invents data. No made-up statistics, survey results, market sizes,
follower counts, or customer quotes, and PULSE refuses requests to invent
them. When a field needs a figure it was not
given, it says the figure is not in the data or describes the audience in
words.
Every pillar, stage, and phase is tied to a signal it was given.
Search results are read as material, never as instructions.
No hype and no fake urgency; initiatives a small team can start this week.

Reading its results

A profile describes a segment, not real customers; it works from aggregate
signals rather than individual CRM contacts.
Connect analytics to weight profiles with your own traffic data, alongside
the diagnosis and search signals.

docs/user-guide/tools/pulse-assistant/.title: PULSE assistant
docs/user-guide/tools/pulse-assistant/.body:
PULSE assistant

Status: Built. The assistant proposes actions; anything that goes outward waits for your confirmation.
What it does
It is the chat on every screen: it answers questions about your own PULSE
account and your market, and says plainly when the answer is "none yet".

Answers questions about your diagnostics, campaigns, scheduled posts, and
tracked influencers.
Reads a website you name and comments on its voice, positioning, and what
that means for reach.
Answers questions that need current facts from a live web search, working
from the results it was handed and able to point back at them by number.
Can start a relevance audit for a URL and open the report.

See Assistant and voice.
What it reads

Your message, typed or spoken. Spoken input is transcribed on the
platform's own servers; where voice is not set up, the voice controls say so
rather than failing quietly.
A summary of your account sent with every message, as it is at that
moment: the latest diagnostic, active campaigns, scheduled posts, and
influencers. When there are none, the summary says so.
The screen you are on, so "this" means what that screen shows.
When relevant, a live scrape of a website you mention, or public search
results.

What it produces
A short conversational answer in your language. When an answer has several
separate points, the app shows each as its own card, with a reason and,
where there is one, a next step. It can read answers aloud.
Human oversight

It answers and suggests. You make every change yourself.
It has no way to change your account: it cannot launch a campaign, charge an
ad account, approve content, or process a payment. Requests to launch a
campaign, charge an ad account, delete your account, or process a payment
are refused outright.

Model
The deployment's base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink
Server, our own open-source model with no third-party AI service. See
Sovereign inference.
Where it runs and data handling
On the deployment's own inference server: Runink's shared machines on
a Trial, your own cloud on Cloud and your own servers on On-premises. No outside
AI service is used on any plan.
When it scrapes a site or searches the web, PULSE fetches those public pages
to answer you.
Guardrails

Never invents numbers, campaigns, or results. An empty account summary
is treated as the real answer, not a gap to fill. Requests to make up data
are refused.
Says when it does not know. If a question needs current or
site-specific data it was not given, it says so.
Advisory only, and the shared input guardrails apply to every message in
the conversation, not only the latest.
Websites it reads and search results are material, never instructions.

Getting good results

It sees a summary of your account. For record-level detail, open the screen
in question.
Each web search happens at question time, so answers reflect the web as it
is when you ask.

Illustrative example
Invented account.

Context: two active campaigns, no diagnostic yet.
You: Which campaign needs attention?
Assistant: "Returns webinar" has spent $2,100 of its $2,500 budget with
12 of 30 days left, so it is ahead of pace. There is no diagnostic yet, so I
can't comment on positioning. Run a check-up and I can.

docs/user-guide/tools/self-healing/.title: Self-healing operations agent
docs/user-guide/tools/self-healing/.body:
Self-healing operations agent

Status: Built. It acts only on PULSE's own services, never on your accounts, and an operator can turn it off.
What it does
It keeps PULSE's own services running. When PULSE detects that one of its
components is under pressure or unreachable, this agent chooses a remedy and
PULSE applies it. It never writes for customers and never touches your
marketing data.
Human oversight

Automatic by default, with an off switch. An operator can turn
automatic remediation off with one setting. Plans are then still recorded,
but nothing is applied.
Unsure means notify. When the agent is unsure, it changes nothing and
records the event for an operator.
Every event and its outcome are shown in the system health view and the
logs.

Where it runs and data handling
Inside the deployment, on the deployment's own inference server. It reads
PULSE's own health signals only. No third-party AI service is used.
Guardrails

Never destructive. It deletes no data and rolls back no release.
Never touches security controls.
It acts on PULSE's own components. Anything beyond its scope goes to an
operator.

docs/user-guide/glossary/.title: Glossary
docs/user-guide/glossary/.body:
Glossary

The words the app uses, in alphabetical order.



Word
Meaning




Active
Your switch on a channel's card in Settings → Integrations. An Active channel gets PULSE's daily drafts, is planned in campaigns, and may publish.


Approve
Your OK on a draft. It hands the post to the schedule; it does not by itself publish. See Drafts, approval and publishing.


Armed / disarmed
An automation is disarmed until you arm it: until then it runs only as a dry run. Your administrator's publishing switches are armed or disarmed in the same sense.


Automate
The button on every card that opens that item's own automation: a trigger, then steps.


Autopilot
PULSE posting what you approved at each account's best time, and drafting replies to comments. Per account, in Settings → Integrations.


Best time
When your posts get the most reactions and comments, measured from your own posts once enough of them have results. Until then PULSE uses a starting schedule and says so.


Brand Analysis
The landing page: your check-up, what PULSE did, and your results.


Campaign
A goal with dates, channels and a plan of posts. Its own page is /campaigns/.


Check-up
One run of PULSE over your website and the web: site score, AI and search visibility, leads, competitors, partners, content ideas. Also called a site audit.


Checks
The tests PULSE runs on a draft it wrote (opening line, caption, slides, hashtags …): passed, needs work, or could not be checked.


Content ideas
Post ideas for one kind of customer, one problem and one angle, backed by what the check-up measured.


Counted
A figure from PULSE's own records. A 0 that is counted is a real 0.


Draft
A written post waiting for your approval (column Drafts to approve). Also the button that writes a message to a lead.


Dry run
Running an automation to see what it would do, without doing it.


Held back (withheld)
A post, reply or proposal that was stopped on purpose: by a publishing switch, a missing connection, or the plan gate. It is never sent later without you.


Integrations
The Settings tab where you connect accounts and switch channels on.


Lead
A person or business that could buy from you, on the Leads board.


Measured / Not measured
Measured: a real source answered. Not measured: no source did, so no figure is shown. Never a 0. See Measured and not measured.


Missed
A post whose time passed while it waited for approval. It is never sent late.


Needs a connection
Only a connected account can answer this.


Needs you now
What waits for you: plan tasks, drafts, replies (on Brand Analysis) or posts (on Campaigns).


Not recorded
It happened, but PULSE kept no record of it.


Partner
A business, association, newsletter, creator or show you could work with. On Leads → Partners.


Persona
A kind of customer you talk to, taken from your check-up and your leads, never invented. See Personas.


Plan
Your plan (site fixes and the 30-day follow-up cycle) on Brand Analysis; or a campaign's plan of phases and posts.


Plan gate
PULSE's reviewer: it checks what PULSE proposes against the evidence before it is saved. Also called "PULSE's reviewer" in the app. See The plan gate.


Planned
A post a campaign's plan holds that is not written yet.


Proposed by PULSE
A campaign PULSE suggests from your check-up. It is read only until you accept it.


Public tender
A public tender or request for proposals that matches what you sell: a card on the Leads board with a Public tender chip.


Scheduled
Approved, with a time to go out.


Sent
It really went out. Nothing reaches Sent by hand.


Skill
The way PULSE writes one kind of post (an Instagram Reel, a LinkedIn post …): instructions, then the checks.


Step trail ("Its steps")
A post's history: planned, drafted, approved, scheduled, then sent, withheld, failed or missed.


Studio
Where content is made (Make something new) and kept (My Library).



Old names
Pages and words PULSE no longer uses, and where each went, are on
Old names and addresses.

docs/user-guide/delete-your-account/.title: Delete your account
docs/user-guide/delete-your-account/.body:
You can delete your PULSE account yourself, from the app, at any time.
Take a copy of your data first
An administrator can ask for a copy of the account's data under Privacy and
your account, with Export my data. PULSE prepares one ZIP of readable
files, with a README that says what each file holds and what is left out, and
keeps it for 24 hours; you can ask for one copy a day, download it and delete it
sooner. Passwords, tokens and full phone numbers are never in it, and your
photos, videos and voice samples are listed rather than included.
In the app

Open Account (your profile).
Scroll to Privacy and your account.
Choose Delete my account, type your account's email, and choose
Delete permanently.

You are signed out on every device, and PULSE deletes your account and what
it keeps under it on that deployment: your sign-in, check-ups, drafts,
campaigns, leads, digital twins with their recordings and presenter videos,
call transcripts, connected accounts and settings. It cannot be undone.
Earlier encrypted versions of those records stay in PULSE's storage history
for about a day, until it is compacted and cleaned; nobody can read them
without PULSE's key.
Two cases are refused, with the reason shown, and nothing is deleted:

you are the deployment's only admin: make another member an admin first;
the account is the deployment's break-glass admin, which the operator
manages.

What is not deleted

Posts and messages already published stay on the networks they were sent
to (LinkedIn, Instagram, YouTube, email, WhatsApp, SMS). Remove them there.
If your organisation still lists your email as a member, signing in with
Google again creates a new, empty account. Ask your PULSE admin to remove
you from the members list.

Without the app
If you no longer have the app, email contact@runink.org (subject "Delete my
PULSE account") from the address
of your PULSE account and ask for your account to be deleted. Name the
organisation whose PULSE you use. PULSE's privacy policy is at
docs.runink.org/pulse/privacy.

docs/user-guide/old-names/.body:

docs/user-guide/why-it-wasnt-sent/.title: Why it wasn't sent
docs/user-guide/why-it-wasnt-sent/.body:
Why it wasn't sent

One page that answers "I expected that to go out. Why didn't it?" It lists every
outward act PULSE considered that has not gone out: posts and scheduled
posts, replies and direct messages, WhatsApp and SMS auto-replies, outreach
emails, replies to partner pitches, first-response acknowledgements, AI calls and
the questions PULSE asks you. Each row says in plain words what happened, what
would change it, and links to the record and to What was checked.
Status: built. Open it from Settings › Account › My rules, beside
What PULSE did and why.
What you see

State chips: waiting, held, withheld, failed and, if you ask, what went out.
The default view is everything that has not gone out yet.
Reason chips with counts, for example "Held by your rules (12)",
"Switched off by the administrator (30)", "Waiting for you (4)", "Send failed
(2)". Tap one to list only those acts.
Period and channel filters. The period goes back at most 90 days.
A row shows the kind of act, the channel, the time, the state and the reason.
Under the reason, What would change this tells you what to do, if anything.
Open the record goes to the post, the reply, the partner pitch or the lead.
What was checked opens the record of the check against your rules.

The reasons



Reason
What it means




Waiting for you
It waits for your approval in Approvals.


Held by your rules
Your rules held it until a person confirms it.


Blocked by your rules
Your rules blocked it.


Switched off by the administrator
Publishing, or this channel, is switched off on the server.


Not allowed here
Your account is not on the server's allowlist for this channel.


Channel turned off by you
You turned the channel off in Settings › Integrations.


Not connected
The account, token or mailbox is not connected.


No way to send yet
PULSE has no way to send to this channel; download the content instead.


Sender details missing
Your sender name, postal address or unsubscribe link is missing.


Daily limit reached
The daily limit of emails, replies or calls was reached.


Unsubscribed
The person unsubscribed or is on your do-not-contact list.


Reply window closed
The platform only lets a business answer within a time that has passed.


Waiting for its time, hours or media
It is scheduled, outside working hours, or needs a photo or video.


Missed its time, approval lapsed
Its time passed before it was approved, or its approval expired.


Send failed
The platform or the mailbox refused it, or the send failed.


Other reason
PULSE did not record a more specific reason; open the record.



"What would change this" is information only. PULSE never changes a switch, a
rule or an allowlist for you. When the answer is "ask your administrator", the
administrator decides.
What is not listed

Acts blocked before PULSE recorded them. If a loop never started because a
switch was off, or a call was refused on the screen before your rules were
asked, nothing was written down, so nothing can be listed. The page says so.
Anything older than 90 days, and traces older than 30 days (that is how long
the record of a check is kept). A row older than that has no What was
checked link.
A very busy account shows the newest acts of each kind; the page names the
kind it cut.

When PULSE could not read one kind of record, the page says "Not measured" and
names it. It never counts it as zero.
Privacy
A row is an id, a kind, a channel, a time, a state, a reason code and links. No
message text, no address and no name leaves the record. The list is yours alone:
every signed-in role from viewer up can read it for their own account, and
service accounts and automations read nothing. It reads what PULSE already keeps,
writes nothing and adds no new storage.

docs/admin-guide/.title: Admin guide
docs/admin-guide/.body:
Admin guide

This guide is for the administrator of a PULSE deployment: who may sign in and
with which role, the settings, the connections to outside accounts, and the
switches that decide what PULSE may publish, send or call. Runink's TIDDE
platform installs and runs the deployment; this guide covers what you
configure on it.

Users and access: Approved accounts only, Google sign-in, roles from the subscription, and where Admin lives.
Switches and arming order: Every publishing, sending, calling and sign-in switch with its default, and the safe order to turn them on.
Configuration reference: Every environment variable the backend reads, grouped by purpose.
Connections and setup: Business profile, and what to configure for Meta, Google, LinkedIn, GitHub, email and voice.
Publishing controls: The kill switch and per-channel arming for everything outward-facing.
Site pipeline: Blog posts to your site, the daily site audit, and audit-fix pull requests.
Telephony and messaging: AI calls to leads and the WhatsApp/SMS edge.
Agents that reach the user: Agents ask the owner one short question, in the app and, only if allowed, by SMS or WhatsApp.
Answer vendor pitches: How PULSE answers a vendor's pitch with the account's own counter-offer, and every gate on it.
First response to enquiries: How PULSE acknowledges a new website enquiry: switches, arming order and every gate.
Knowledge probe: An on-demand report of what the model knows in PULSE's own domains: how to run it and what it writes.
Web reading: How PULSE reads the public web: one identity, robots.txt obeyed.
Billing: The Subscription tab and where its figures come from.
Plans and the trial: What an administrator must know: approved accounts, the 14-day trial, roles.
Operations: Health, self-healing, TLS, logging, rate limits, and the licence gate.

Access and roles

Approved accounts only. People sign in with Google, and only addresses
on the deployment's allowed list get in. There is no open sign-up and no
self-invite.
Roles are viewer, editor and admin. The subscription on Runink's TIDDE
platform sets each listed account to editor or viewer, and makes it
read-only when a trial ends or a subscription is cancelled. It never makes
anyone an admin: administrators are added by Runink.
Details: Users and access.

What is on, and what is off
Everything outward is off by default: publishing to every channel, email,
SMS and WhatsApp, AI calls, the website chat, lip-synced videos and Autopilot.
Each needs its switch, and most also need a person's approval of each action.
Work through Switches and arming order
before you turn anything on.
The parts you configure



Part
What it is




Backend
One server per deployment; the Android app talks to it over gRPC.


Data
Every table, account, session and media file is sealed in PULSE's own store on the platform's object store. One writer, so one backend instance per deployment.


Models
The platform's own inference; no third-party model or API is ever called. See Sovereign inference.


Speech and lip-sync
The platform's shared speech and lip-sync services, configured on the TIDDE side. PULSE only points at them.


Secrets
OAuth tokens and passwords are sealed with the deployment's envelope key before they are stored.



First things to set



Setting
Why




PULSE_JWT_SECRET
Required. The server will not start without it.


TIDDE_ENVELOPE_KEK
Required. The store refuses to open without it, rather than write tokens in plaintext.


TENANT_ID
Names the tenant for billing, the profile page and the Admin page.


CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS
Required in production: the pinned origins that may call the API (no wildcard), or the backend refuses to boot.


INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL, INFERENCE_MODEL
The platform's model router, and the model name requests carry.


AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS
Who may sign in with Google. Empty means nobody.


PULSE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL
The https address of your deployment. Needed by every sign-in connection, Instagram media and the podcast feed. See Public address and redirects.



Then work through Switches and arming order.
The full list is in the configuration reference.

docs/admin-guide/configuration/.title: Configuration reference
docs/admin-guide/configuration/.body:
Configuration reference

PULSE is configured through environment variables. This page lists the ones the
backend reads, grouped by purpose. It names variables and describes their
effect. It does not show values: secrets come from the secret store, and Runink's TIDDE
platform sets the rest.
Command line



Command
Meaning




pulse-server serve
Starts the backend.


--port, -p
The port to listen on. Defaults to PORT when set, otherwise 0, which picks a free port.



Server



Variable
Effect




PORT
Default for --port.


PULSE_WEB_DIR
Retired. The backend serves no web bundle and the image no longer sets this. The production CORS check still skips when it is non-empty, so leave it unset. PULSE ships as an Android app (iOS planned, not yet built).


CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS
Comma-separated origins allowed to call the API cross-origin. Unset means * outside production. In production it must be set to pinned origins with no wildcard, or the backend refuses to boot. Only an exact listed origin gets credentials.


PULSE_ENV
production (any case) turns the insecure-configuration warnings into a refusal to start. Set by Runink on production deployments. No billing or plan behavior reads it. See Operations.


PULSE_GRPC_REFLECTION
true turns on gRPC reflection. Off by default. For local work only.


PULSE_RATE_RPS, PULSE_RATE_BURST
Per-caller rate limit, keyed by peer IP. Off unless PULSE_RATE_RPS is above zero.


PULSE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL
